    Unit 2

    Binary Decision Making

    Theory

    1Digital artifacts and the four kinds of media

    A digital artifact is anything you make on a computer and save as a file: a story, a poster, a slideshow, a voice recording, a video. Artifacts are built from four kinds of media — text, images, audio and video. Last year you made simple artifacts with one kind of media; this year you make advanced ones that mix several — your internet-safety video will have moving pictures, your voice, music and words on the screen at the same time.

    Text, image, audio, video — and the file extensions that usually go with each.

    Every artifact lives in a file. A file has a name you choose and an extension the computer adds after the dot — .mp4 means video, .jpg means picture. Name your files so future-you can find them: internet-safety-video-v2.mp4 beats untitled(3).mp4.

    2Hardware and software compatibility

    Hardware is the machine you can touch (laptop, tablet, USB stick, camera). Software is the program running on it (Canva, PowerPoint, a photo app). Compatible means “works together”. A file made in one program may not open in another: a .pptx needs PowerPoint or Google Slides; a video from an iPhone (.mov) may not play on an old Windows laptop; a Canva design only opens in Canva unless you download it as .mp4 or .pdf.

    You made…Saved asOpens inSafe to send as
    A slideshow.pptxPowerPoint, Google Slides.pdf
    A Canva design(online only)Canva.png / .pdf / .mp4
    A video on an iPhone.movApple apps, most players.mp4
    A voice recording.m4a / .wavmost players.mp3
    A Scratch project.sb3Scratch only.sb3 (they need Scratch)

    Common formats travel well; program-only formats need the same program at the other end.

    The safe habit: before sending a file, ask “What will they open it with?” When unsure, export to a common format that almost everything opens — .pdf for documents, .jpg/.png for pictures, .mp4 for video, .mp3 for sound. Hardware can be incompatible too: a USB-C stick will not fit an older USB-A port without an adapter.

    3Transferring files between devices

    A file on your laptop is not on your tablet until you transfer it. Four ways: a USB stick (copy the file on, plug into the other device, copy off — no internet needed); the cloud (upload to Google Drive or iCloud, then open it anywhere you sign in); an attachment in email or chat (fine for small files); and short-range wireless like AirDrop, Bluetooth or Nearby Share (two devices next to each other).

    Four roads for the same file. The file is COPIED — the original stays where it was.

    Choose by size and distance: a 2 GB video will not go through email (most limit attachments to about 25 MB) — use the cloud or a USB stick. Two tablets in the same room → AirDrop. A file for a friend in another city → cloud link. Always keep the original until you have checked the copy opens.

    4Published instantly, seen by anyone: your digital footprint

    When you press “Post”, your picture or message is published instantly — within one second it is copied to a company’s server and to every friend’s screen. From there it can be screenshotted, forwarded and found by search engines. Everything you leave online — posts, comments, likes, photos, even the games you play — is your digital footprint. Unlike footprints in sand, it does not wash away.

    One post, many copies, no “undo”. This is why we think BEFORE we post.

    So the question is never “can I delete it later?” but “would I be happy for anyone — a teacher, a stranger, future me — to see this?” If not, don’t post. Good footprints exist too: a kind comment, a drawing you are proud of, a science project — those are worth leaving.

    5Staying safe online: the SMART rules

    Five rules that fit on one hand. Safe — keep personal information (full name, address, school, phone, passwords) private. Meet — never meet someone you only know online without a trusted adult. Accepting — don’t open files, links or messages from people you don’t know. Reliable — not everything online is true; check with a grown-up or a second source. Tell — if anything online makes you feel worried, sad or scared, tell a trusted adult straight away. These five rules are the heart of your safety video.

    LetterRuleExample
    SafeKeep personal information privatefull name, address, school, passwords
    MeetNever meet an online “friend” without an adulta stranger from a game asks to meet
    AcceptingDon’t open files or links from people you don’t know“Click here for a free prize!”
    ReliableNot everything online is true — checka video that says dolphins can fly
    TellTell a trusted adult if something worries yousomeone sends a mean message

    SMART: five rules, five scenes for your video.

    6Typing fluency: the home row

    Fast, accurate typing frees your brain for ideas. The secret is the home row: left fingers rest on A S D F, right fingers on J K L ;, thumbs on the space bar. Every other key is a short reach from there, and your fingers return home after each press. The tiny bumps on F and J let you find home without looking — so keep your eyes on the screen, not the keyboard.

    Each finger owns a home key and the keys above and below it.

    We measure typing with WPM (words per minute, counting 5 letters as a word) and accuracy (how many letters were right). Accuracy comes first — a fast typist who makes mistakes spends longer fixing them. Sit straight, wrists floating, and practise 5 minutes a day in the Lab tab.

    ExtraBeyond the basics: how big is a file?

    File size is measured in bytes. 1 000 bytes ≈ 1 KB (kilobyte), 1 000 KB ≈ 1 MB (megabyte), 1 000 MB ≈ 1 GB (gigabyte). A page of text is a few KB, a photo is 2–5 MB, one minute of phone video is about 100 MB, and a USB stick holds 16–128 GB. This is why video is the hardest media to send by email — and why the cloud and USB sticks exist.

    ▸Show hintHide hint

    Example 3

    Lan posts a photo of her class in front of the school sign with the caption “Class 4A, Vinschool, back at 3 pm every day!” — then deletes it ten minutes later. Trace what may have happened in those ten minutes, and explain which SMART rule was broken.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Publication is instant: who received a copy in the first second?
    2. What information does the caption give a stranger?
    3. Which letter of SMART is about personal information?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: within seconds the photo was copied to the platform’s server and to followers’ phones; anyone could have screenshotted it. Deleting removed only Lan’s copy. The caption reveals her school, class and daily time — the S (Safe) rule: keep personal information private. Also the photo shows classmates’ faces without asking them (Ask an adult first).

    Practice

    Theory

    1Algorithms have three building blocks

    An algorithm is a set of clear, step-by-step instructions to do a task — like a recipe or the rules of a game. In Year 3 you built algorithms with sequence (steps one after another) and repetition (loops that do something again and again). This unit adds the third building block: selection — the computer chooses what to do next based on a question.

    Sequence runs steps in order · Selection picks ONE of two paths · Repetition goes round again.

    The word binary means “made of two”. A binary decision is a decision with exactly two possible answers: yes or no, true or false. Every IF block in Scratch makes a binary decision — that is why the unit is called Binary Decision Making.

    2Selection: IF a condition is true, THEN do something

    Selection always starts with a condition — a question whose answer is true or false. “Is it raining?” “Is the answer yes?” “Is the score bigger than 5?” If the condition is true, the computer runs the THEN part. We can draw this as a flowchart: the diamond shape is the question, and the two arrows leaving it are the two possible paths.

    A flowchart for getting ready to go out. The diamond is the condition; YES and NO are the two paths.

    Follow the flowchart with your finger. Start at the top, answer the question honestly, and follow only the arrow that matches your answer. Notice that you never walk both paths — a binary decision picks exactly one.

    3IF … THEN versus IF … THEN … ELSE

    Scratch has two selection blocks in the orange Control group. The if … then block has one “door”: when the condition is true the blocks inside run; when it is false, nothing happens and the program simply carries on. The if … then … else block has two doors: the top part runs when the condition is true, the else part runs when it is false. Exactly one of the two doors is always used.

    if … then (one door)

    when 🏁 clicked
    ask Do you like ice cream? and wait
    if answer = yes then
    say Me too!

    answer “no” → nothing happens, the sprite stays silent.

    if … then … else (two doors)

    when 🏁 clicked
    ask Do you like ice cream? and wait
    if answer = yes then
    say Me too!
    else
    say Oh, really?

    answer “no” → the ELSE part runs: “Oh, really?”

    Same question, two different blocks. Only the right-hand script answers the child who says “no”.

    Use if … then when you only want to react to a “yes”. Use if … then … else when both answers need a reply — for example a quiz that must say “Correct!” or “Wrong!”.

    4Conditions and comparison operators

    A condition compares two things. The green Operators group gives us three comparison operators: = (equal to), > (greater than) and < (less than). Each one is a pointed, six-sided block — the shape tells you it always reports true or false, so it fits exactly into the pointed hole of an IF block. A true/false value is called a Boolean.

    BlockQuestion it asksExampleResult
    a = bAre they the same?7 = 7true
    a > bIs the left one bigger?3 > 10false
    a < bIs the left one smaller?3 < 10true
    a = bSame word? (capitals don’t matter)YES = yestrue

    The three comparison blocks. Try each example in the Lab tab — drop the block into an IF and watch which door opens.

    Two rules to remember. First, = works with words as well as numbers, and Scratch ignores capital letters — “YES” = “yes” is true. Second, extra letters or spaces spoil the match — “yes please” = “yes” is false. When the answer must be a number, use > or <: “answer > 10” is true for 11, 50 or 999 but false for 10 itself.

    5A whole program: purpose, event, input, decision, outcome

    Before building, a good programmer writes down the purpose of the program (what is it for?) and the expected outcome (what should the user see?). Every Scratch program starts with an event — a hat block such as when 🏁 clicked or when space key pressed. It often takes an input with the ask … and wait block: whatever the user types is stored in the light-blue answer block. Then a decision block checks the answer and produces an output, usually with say.

    when 🏁 clicked
    set score ▾ to 0
    ask Is a spider an insect? and wait
    if answer = no then
    change score ▾ by 1
    say Correct! for 2 seconds
    else
    say Wrong — a spider has 8 legs! for 2 seconds
    say join Your score: score

    Top: the four parts of a program. Bottom: a one-question Yes/No quiz written with Scratch blocks.

    Here is the full Yes/No quiz script you will build in the Lab. Read it from top to bottom: event → set score to 0 → ask → decide → say the score. A variable (orange) is a named box that remembers a number — perfect for keeping score.

    6Follow, predict, fix and evaluate a program

    You do not need to run a program to know what it will do. Tracing means reading the blocks one by one and writing down what happens for a given input — a trace table keeps it tidy. Tracing helps you predict the outcome, and it is the fastest way to find a bug (a mistake in the code). Common bugs with selection: comparing with the wrong word (“Yes!” instead of “yes”), using > when you meant =, or putting the say block outside the IF so it runs every time.

    A trace table for “if answer = yes then say Correct! else say Try again”. Row 4 shows a sneaky bug: extra words break the match.

    Finally, evaluate the program against its criteria — a checklist written from the purpose. For the quiz: Does it ask a question? Does it reply to both yes and no? Does it keep score? Does it show the score at the end? A program is finished when every box is ticked — not when it “looks done”.

    ExtraBeyond the basics: two conditions at once

    Sometimes one question is not enough. You can put an IF inside another IF (this is called nesting), or join two conditions with the green and / or blocks. “answer > 0 and answer < 10” is true only for numbers between 1 and 9. “answer = yes or answer = y” accepts either spelling. The not block flips true into false.

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Trace this script. The player types no. What does the sprite say, in order?

    when 🏁 clicked
    ask Is 7 an odd number? and wait
    if answer = yes then
    say Correct! 7 is odd. for 2 seconds
    else
    say Not quite — 7 is odd. for 2 seconds
    say Thanks for playing!
    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Start at the hat block and go down one block at a time. The ask block shows the question and waits — the answer is “no”.
    2. The IF checks answer = yes. Is “no” the same as “yes”? No → the condition is false, so skip the THEN part and run the ELSE part.
    3. After the IF block finishes, the program carries on with the next block underneath, whatever happened inside.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: “Not quite — 7 is odd.” for 2 seconds, then “Thanks for playing!”. The THEN part (“Correct!”) never runs, because the condition was false.
    Example 2

    This quiz never says “What is its name?” even when the player types yes. Find the bug and fix it.

    when 🏁 clicked
    ask Do you have a pet? and wait
    if answer > yes then
    say What is its name?
    else
    say Maybe one day!
    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Look at the condition inside the IF. Which comparison operator is being used?
    2. > asks “is the left bigger than the right?”. That makes sense for numbers, but “yes” is a word — we want to know if it is the same word.
    3. Swap the operator for the one that checks “are they equal?”.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: the condition should be answer = yes, not answer > yes. The > block compares sizes, so “yes > yes” is always false and the ELSE door always opens.
    Example 3

    The purpose of this program is: “a one-question quiz that tells the player if they are right or wrong”. Evaluate it against these criteria: (1) asks a question, (2) replies to a correct answer, (3) replies to a wrong answer, (4) uses selection.

    when 🏁 clicked
    ask Is the Sun a star? and wait
    if answer = yes then
    say Correct! for 2 seconds
    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Go through the criteria one by one and look for the block that meets each one.
    2. (1) The ask block asks a question ✔. (2) When answer = yes, it says “Correct!” ✔. (4) There is an IF block ✔.
    3. (3) What happens when the player types “no”? Trace it: the condition is false, there is no ELSE… so nothing is said.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: it meets criteria 1, 2 and 4 but FAILS criterion 3 — a wrong answer gets no reply. Fix: replace if … then with if … then … else and put say “Wrong — the Sun is a star!” in the ELSE part.

    Practice

    Theory

    1What is data — and what is information?

    Data is a collection of facts you can record: numbers (8 dogs), words (“Dog”), yes/no answers, measurements (27 °C). A single piece on its own says little — “6” means nothing until you know it is “6 pupils chose Cat”. When data is organised and explained so that it answers a question, it becomes information: “Dogs are the most popular pet in 4A”. Computers are brilliant at storing and adding up data; you turn it into information by asking good questions.

    The data cycle. Every project in this unit walks through all five boxes.

    Data comes in two flavours. Quantitative data is numbers you can add and average (age, height, hours of sleep, number of pets). Qualitative data is categories or descriptions (favourite colour, pet type, “I like it because…”). Both are useful — but you can only calculate an average from numbers. This unit follows a five-step data cycle: question → collect → organise → chart → conclude.

    2Collecting data: surveys and good questions

    A survey asks many people the same questions so you can count the answers. Online forms (Google Forms) do the counting for you: every answer lands in a spreadsheet automatically. The quality of your data depends on the quality of your questions. Closed questions (choose one, tick boxes, type a number) are easy to count. Open questions (“Tell me about…”) give rich answers but are hard to chart. A leading question pushes people toward an answer and makes the data unfair.

    QuestionTypeGood for a survey?
    “Do you have a pet? ☐ Yes ☐ No”Closed (choice)✅ Easy to count
    “Which pet? ☐ Dog ☐ Cat ☐ Fish ☐ Bird ☐ Other”Closed (multiple choice)✅ “Other” means nobody is stuck
    “How many hours do you sleep? (number)”Number✅ Can average it
    “Tell me about your pet.”Open⚠️ Interesting but hard to count
    “Don’t you agree dogs are the best pet?”Leading❌ Unfair — pushes the answer

    Five question types. The first three give data you can count; the last one spoils the data.

    Rules for a fair survey: ask everyone the same questions in the same way; include an “Other” option so nobody is forced to pick wrong; ask enough people (a sample of 3 friends tells you about 3 friends, not about the school); and never collect personal data you do not need — no full names, no addresses (remember SMART from Unit 1).

    3Organising data: tables and spreadsheets

    Collected data goes into a table: one row per thing (a pet type, a pupil, a day) and one column per fact about it (name, count, temperature). The first row is the header — the column names. A spreadsheet (Google Sheets, Excel) is a table that can calculate. Columns are lettered A, B, C…; rows are numbered 1, 2, 3…; each box is a cell named by its column and row — B3 is column B, row 3.

    Columns have letters, rows have numbers, cells have both. The green cell holds a formula.

    A range is a block of cells written first:last — B2:B4 means B2, B3 and B4. Ranges are how you tell a formula “use all of these”. Tips: type one value per cell (never “8 dogs” in one cell — put “Dog” in A and 8 in B); keep numbers as numbers so the spreadsheet can add them; and sort a column (biggest first) to see the winner instantly.

    4Formulas: let the computer do the maths

    A formula is an instruction typed into a cell that starts with =. The cell then shows the result, and updates by itself whenever the data changes. The four you need: =SUM(B2:B6) adds the range; =AVERAGE(B2:B6) finds the mean (total ÷ how many); =MAX(B2:B6) picks the biggest; =MIN(B2:B6) the smallest. You can also do plain arithmetic: =B2+B3, =B2*2, =B7/5.

    FormulaMeansWith B2:B4 = 8, 6, 4
    =SUM(B2:B4)add them all18
    =AVERAGE(B2:B4)total ÷ how many18 ÷ 3 = 6
    =MAX(B2:B4)the biggest8
    =MIN(B2:B4)the smallest4
    =COUNT(B2:B4)how many numbers3
    =B2-B4plain subtraction4

    The formula toolbox. Each one starts with = and names a range in brackets.

    Why formulas instead of typing the total? Because data changes. If one more pupil joins and says “Dog”, you change B2 from 8 to 9 and the total, the average and the chart all fix themselves. A typed “18” would silently become wrong. Formula habit: never type a number you could calculate.

    5Charts: choosing the right picture

    A chart turns a table into a picture so a reader sees the pattern in one second. A bar chart uses bars of different heights to compare amounts — the best all-round choice. A pie chart cuts a circle into slices to show parts of a whole (what fraction chose Dog) — only use it when the pieces add up to everything. A pictogram uses little pictures, each standing for a number of things (🐶 = 2 pets) — friendly for young readers, but it must have a key.

    One table, three charts. Ask “compare? part of whole? over time?” before choosing.

    Every good chart has: a title that says what it shows, labels on the axes (what and in what unit), and a scale that starts at zero — a bar chart whose axis starts at 5 makes a difference of 1 look huge. If you have data that changes over time (temperature each day), a line chart is best because the line shows the trend.

    6Analysing: what does the data say?

    Analysing means reading the table or chart and stating what you found, with numbers: “Dog is the most popular (8 of 25 pupils, about one third). Bird is the least (2). More pupils have no pet (5) than have a bird.” Then draw a conclusion that answers your original question — and be honest about the limits: 25 pupils in one class is not the whole school. A good analysis ends with a new question: “Would Year 2 choose the same?”

    Watch for tricks: a chart with no title or key is a guess; a pie chart of things that do not add to a whole is nonsense; a survey of 3 people proves nothing; and “most popular” with 8 of 25 still means 17 chose something else. Being a careful reader of data is as important as making it.

    ExtraBeyond the basics: big data

    Your survey has 25 rows. Vietnam’s 2019 census had one row for each of 96.2 million people — collected by 122 000 enumerators with tablets. Weather services record millions of measurements every hour; a hospital stores every heartbeat from a monitor. Such big data is far too large for a human to read, so computers search it for patterns — the same idea as your SUM and MAX, just billions of times faster. That is why learning to ask a clear question and choose the right chart matters: the tools scale up, the thinking stays the same.

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Class 4A counted their pets: Dog 8, Cat 6, Fish 4, Bird 2, None 5. The numbers are in B2:B6. Write the formulas for the total, the average, and the most popular count, and say what each shows.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Which cells hold the numbers? Write the range first:last.
    2. Total = SUM. Average = total ÷ how many. Biggest = MAX.
    3. Do the maths by hand to check: 8+6+4+2+5 = ?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: =SUM(B2:B6) shows 25 (25 pupils answered). =AVERAGE(B2:B6) shows 5 (25 ÷ 5 groups). =MAX(B2:B6) shows 8 — the Dog count. Note that MAX gives the number 8, not the word “Dog”; you read the label next to it.
    Example 2

    Minh wants to show (a) which snack is most popular in his class, and (b) what fraction of pupils walk to school. Which chart type fits each, and why?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. (a) is about COMPARING amounts between snacks.
    2. (b) is about a PART of the WHOLE class.
    3. Bar = compare; pie = parts of a whole.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: (a) a bar chart — tall bar = popular snack, easy to compare five or six snacks. (b) a pie chart — the whole circle is the class; the “walk” slice shows the fraction at a glance (e.g. one quarter). A pie for (a) would also work since every pupil picks one snack, but bars make “which is biggest” clearer.
    Example 3

    Lan surveyed 3 friends: “Don’t you think maths is the best subject?” All three said yes. She concludes: “Everyone in the school loves maths most.” Find three problems with her survey.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Look at the question wording — does it push an answer?
    2. Look at how many people — is 3 enough for a school?
    3. Look at who — are 3 friends like the whole school?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: (1) It is a leading question — “Don’t you think…” pushes people to agree. A fair version: “Which subject do you like most? ☐ Maths ☐ English ☐ Science ☐ Art ☐ Other”. (2) The sample is too small — 3 people cannot represent hundreds. (3) The sample is not fair — her friends may share her tastes; ask pupils from different classes. Her conclusion is far bigger than her data.

    Practice

    Theory

    1How computers help society — and the risks

    Computers are everywhere, doing two kinds of good. They help society — many people at once: weather computers warn a whole city of a storm, traffic lights timed by computers cut jams, hospital scanners let doctors see inside the body, robots do dangerous factory jobs. And they help individuals: a phone reads text aloud to a blind person, a farmer’s app says when to water the rice, you video-call grandparents far away, a learning app lets you practise maths at your own pace.

    Helps society 🌍Helps one person 🙋Risk ⚠️
    Storm warnings for a cityPhone reads text aloudToo much screen time
    Smart traffic lightsVideo call to grandparentsStrangers pretending to be friends
    Robots in dangerous factoriesLearning app at your own paceFake news spreading

    Sort any example into one of three boxes — the Lab’s sorting game trains exactly this.

    But every tool has risks. Too much screen time hurts sleep and eyes; strangers can pretend to be friends online; fake news spreads faster than true news; computers that decide things (who gets a loan, which video you see next) can be unfair if their data is unfair. A good designer asks three questions about anything they build: Who does it help? Who could it hurt? How do we make it safe?

    2What is a robot? Sense, think, act

    A robot is a machine that can sense the world, think (run a program) and act on its own. A washing machine acts but does not sense much; a thermometer senses but does not act; a robot vacuum does all three: its bump sensor feels a wall, its program decides “turn”, its motors turn the wheels — then it senses again. That loop, repeated thousands of times a second, is what makes a robot seem clever.

    Sense → think → act → repeat. Cover any one box and it is no longer a robot.

    Robot parts match the loop. Sensors sense: camera, microphone, distance (ultrasound), bump, temperature, light. The controller thinks: a tiny computer running your program — the same if/then decisions you wrote in Unit 2. Actuators act: motors, wheels, tracks, legs, propellers, a gripper arm, a speaker, a screen. A power source (battery, solar panel) and a body hold it all together. Choose each part for the job: tracks for rough ground, propellers for flying, a gripper for picking up.

    3Designing a robot to solve a problem

    Designers do not start with “a cool robot”; they start with a problem and a user. The design process has five steps: Problem (what is difficult, for whom, where) → User (what they need: quiet? small? cheap?) → Design (choose sensors, movement and tools that fit; sketch it) → Build a model (in this unit, a 3D model in Tinkercad) → Test & improve (does it solve the problem? change one thing and test again). This is the same evaluate-and-improve loop you used in Units 1 and 2.

    StepQuestion to answerExample: DustBuddy
    1 ProblemWho has what difficulty? Where?Crumbs under the dining table after dinner
    2 UserWho will use it? What do they need?A busy family; must be quiet and safe around the cat
    3 DesignWhich sensors, movement, tools?Low round body, wheels, bump + distance sensors, brush + vacuum, battery
    4 BuildMake a model (Tinkercad) or prototypeCylinder + box + two cylinder wheels, grouped
    5 Test & improveDoes it solve the problem? What to change?Too tall for under the chairs → make it lower

    Five steps, one example. Your Lab task 4 and the Tinkercad project follow this table.

    A strong design explains why each part is there: “distance sensor so it does not fall down the stairs; brush because crumbs stick to the carpet; low round body to fit under chairs.” If you cannot say why a part is there, it probably should not be.

    4Editing digital images

    A digital image is a grid of tiny coloured squares called pixels. Image editors (Canva, Photos, Paint, Pixlr) change those pixels. The basic edits: crop cuts away the edges to keep only the part you want (removes clutter, changes the shape); resize makes the picture smaller or larger (smaller = fewer pixels = smaller file — good for email and websites); rotate and flip turn it; brightness makes everything lighter or darker; contrast makes dark parts darker and light parts lighter so the picture looks crisp; filters such as grayscale change the colours.

    pixels. A phone photo has about 12 million of them.

    Four edits you will do in the Lab’s image editor, and the pixels underneath every picture.

    Two rules. Enlarging cannot add detail: a small picture stretched big goes blurry, because the editor has to invent pixels. So always keep the original and shrink copies, never the reverse. And edit with a purpose: a poster picture needs a crop that points at the subject and enough brightness to read; a robot photo for your design page needs the background removed, not a rainbow filter. Save the edited copy with a new name (robot-v2.png).

    53D design in Tinkercad

    Tinkercad (tinkercad.com) is a free website for building 3D models from simple shapes: box, cylinder, sphere, cone, wedge. You drag a shape onto the workplane, resize it with the white handles, lift it with the black cone handle, and rotate it with the curved arrows. The magic tool is Hole: turn a shape into a hole, overlap it with a solid, and Group them — the hole is cut out. That is how you make wheels with axles, a body with a slot for the battery, or eyes in a head.

    You want…Do this in Tinkercad
    A robot bodyDrag a Box, set 40 × 30 × 20 mm with the handles
    WheelsCylinder → rotate 90° → Ctrl+D to copy
    Eyes / a slotSmall shape → click Hole → overlap → select both → Group
    Everything lined upSelect all → L (Align) → click the centre dots
    Name and saveClick the name top-left → rename; Tinkercad saves automatically
    3D print / shareExport → .STL, or Share → screenshot

    The six moves that build any robot model. Solid + Hole + Group is the one to remember.

    Useful habits: Align (press L) lines shapes up perfectly instead of by eye; the ruler shows real sizes in mm; Ctrl+D duplicates (make one wheel, duplicate three times); and Export gives an .stl file a 3D printer can print. Tinkercad is free; children under 13 join a teacher’s class with a code or with a parent’s approval.

    6Being a responsible designer

    Designers shape how people live, so they carry responsibility. Ask: is my robot safe (no sharp edges, stops when it bumps a child)? Is it fair (usable by someone who cannot see or walk)? Is it honest (does the design page show what it really does)? Does it respect privacy (a camera robot in the house — who sees the video)? And what happens when it breaks or its battery dies — can it be recycled? Good technology is not only clever; it is kind.

    ExtraBeyond the basics: a short history of robots

    The word robot was invented in 1920 by the Czech writer Karel Čapek for his play R.U.R. — from robota, meaning hard work. The first industrial robot, Unimate, started lifting hot metal parts in a car factory in 1961. The Roomba vacuum (2002) brought robots into homes — over 50 million sold. The da Vinci surgical robot (2000) has helped in more than 10 million operations, with a surgeon controlling its arms. Today’s robots deliver parcels, explore Mars and swim under the sea — each one still just sense → think → act.

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Grandma’s plants on the balcony dry out when the family travels. Design a robot to solve this: name the problem and user, then choose ONE sensor, ONE way to move (or none), ONE tool and a power source — and say why each.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Problem: plants dry out. User: Grandma — so it must be simple.
    2. What does the robot need to SENSE to know the soil is dry?
    3. Does it need to move at all if the pots are in one place? What should it ACT with?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    One good answer: Problem — balcony plants dry out for a week. User — Grandma, so it must work with one button. Sensor — a soil-moisture (wetness) sensor in each pot, or a temperature sensor as a simpler stand-in. Movement — none; the pots do not move, so a fixed robot with a hose to each pot is cheaper and safer. Tool — a water sprayer/pump. Power — a solar panel, because the balcony is sunny and there is no plug. Program: if soil is dry then spray for 5 seconds.
    Example 2

    Nam photographed his robot model on a messy desk. The photo is dark, the robot is small in the corner, and the file is 6 MB — too big for the class website. List the edits, in order, and explain each.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Which edit removes the messy desk AND makes the robot bigger in the frame?
    2. Which edit fixes “dark”?
    3. Which edit fixes “6 MB”? Do it LAST — why?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: (1) Crop to the robot — removes the desk clutter and fills the frame with the subject. (2) Brightness up and a little contrast — lifts the dark photo and makes edges crisp. (3) Resize down (e.g. to 1200 pixels wide) — fewer pixels, file drops to well under 1 MB. Resize last so you crop and adjust on the full-detail original. Save as robot-web.jpg; keep the original.
    Example 3

    In Tinkercad, how do you make a robot head (a box) with two round eye sockets? Write the steps.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Start with the solid shape.
    2. Eyes are holes — which tool makes a shape a hole?
    3. What must you do after overlapping a hole with a solid?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: (1) Drag a Box onto the workplane; size it 30 × 30 × 30 mm. (2) Drag a Cylinder, make it 8 mm across, rotate it 90° so it points into the face, and click Hole. (3) Move it into the front of the box; press Ctrl+D and slide the copy sideways for the second eye. (4) Select the box and both cylinders → Group. The cylinders vanish and leave two round sockets. (5) Use L (Align) if the eyes are not level.

    Practice

    Theory

    1Variables: boxes with names

    A variable is a named box in the computer’s memory that holds one value — a number or some text — and can change while the program runs. score, aqi, total, count are variables. In Scratch you make one with Variables → Make a Variable, give it a clear name, and then use three blocks: set (put a new value in the box, replacing the old), change by (add to what is there — use a negative number to subtract), and the round orange reporter that reads the value out.

    The same box after set 0, change by 1, change by 10.

    Naming matters: aqi tells you what is inside, x does not. A variable keeps its value until you change it — so at the start of a program always set counters and totals to 0, or last run’s value will still be in the box. The stage can show a variable’s value in a little monitor (tick the box next to it) — very handy for watching a program count.

    2Arithmetic operators

    The green Operators palette holds the maths. + − × ÷ work on any two numbers or variables, and you can nest them: (a × 10) + b. Two blocks are new and powerful: mod gives the remainder after division (7 mod 2 = 1, 8 mod 2 = 0 — so x mod 2 = 0 means “x is even”); round and floor turn decimals into whole numbers (7 ÷ 2 = 3.5; round → 4; floor → 3). The join block glues text and numbers together for tidy output: join “Total: ” total.

    BlockDoesExample
    3 + 4add3 + 4 → 7
    10 − 4subtract10 − 4 → 6
    6 × 7multiply6 × 7 → 42
    7 ÷ 2divide7 ÷ 2 → 3.5
    7 mod 2remainder after dividing7 mod 2 → 1
    round 3.5round to nearest wholeround 3.5 → 4
    floor ▾ of 3.9drop the decimals (floor)floor of 3.9 → 3
    join AQI 42join textjoin “AQI ” 42 → AQI 42

    The eight operator blocks you will use in this unit.

    Order matters exactly as in maths class: Scratch calculates the inner block first. To compute “average of a, b, c” you need ((a + b) + c) ÷ 3 — three nested blocks. Build from the inside out: make a + b, drop it into the left slot of another +, add c, drop that whole thing into the left slot of ÷.

    3Input → variable → output

    Almost every number program has the same shape: ask the user for a number, store the answer in a variable straight away, calculate, then say the result. Store immediately because Scratch has only one answer box — the next ask overwrites it. Two inputs need two asks and two variables: ask “Length?” → set length to answer → ask “Width?” → set width to answer → say length × width.

    when 🏁 clicked
    ask Length? and wait
    set length ▾ to answer
    ask Width? and wait
    set width ▾ to answer
    set area ▾ to length × width
    say join Area: area

    Ask → set → ask → set → calculate → say. Memorise this skeleton.

    Output should be readable: say 42 is mysterious; say join “Area: ” 42 is clear. In contests the opposite rule applies — print exactly what the examples show, nothing more. Always look at the sample output before writing the say block.

    4Comparing numbers and ranges: the Air Quality Index

    Unit 2 taught yes/no decisions with < = >. With numbers you often need ranges — “between 51 and 100”. The Air Quality Index (AQI) is the perfect example: a number from 0 to 500 that Hanoi’s air sensors report every hour, split into six levels. A range test needs two comparisons joined by and: aqi > 50 and aqi < 101. Or you chain if/else blocks from the top: if aqi < 51 → Good; else if aqi < 101 → Moderate; else if aqi < 151 → … — each test only runs if the earlier ones failed, so one comparison per level is enough.

    The six official AQI levels. Your unit project turns a number into one of these.

    The dangerous places are the edge values: 50 is Good, 51 is Moderate. Scratch has no ≤ block, so “aqi ≤ 50” is written aqi < 51 for whole numbers (or not aqi > 50). Also decide what to do with invalid input — a negative number or 600 is not an AQI; a good program says “Invalid” instead of guessing.

    5Loops that count: repeat + change by

    A loop repeats blocks. Put a variable inside and you can count: set n to 0 → repeat 10 → change n by 1 → say n counts 1 to 10. Add a second variable to keep a running total: set total to 0 → repeat 5 → ask a number → change total by answer — then say total ÷ 5 gives the average of five numbers. This is exactly SUM and AVERAGE from Unit 3, built by hand.

    when 🏁 clicked
    set total ▾ to 0
    set count ▾ to 0
    repeat 5
    ask Number? and wait
    change total ▾ by answer
    change count ▾ by 1
    say join Average: total ÷ count

    A running total inside a loop, then divide by the count: AVERAGE by hand.

    repeat until loops while a condition is false — useful when you do not know how many times: repeat until answer = 0. A counter variable plus a multiplication gives times tables: repeat 10 → change i by 1 → say join i (join “ × 7 = ” i × 7). Watch out for the two classic bugs: forgetting to set the counter to 0 first, and changing by 0 (loop runs forever).

    6Testing number programs

    Numbers hide bugs. Test every program with a test table: a normal value, each edge value (the boundary of every range: 50 and 51 for AQI), the smallest allowed input (0 or 1), a big input, and an invalid one (−5, 600, or a word). Write the expected output before running, then compare. If the program says “Moderate” for 50, the comparison is off by one — the most common mistake in the whole unit.

    Input (aqi)Expected output
    42Good
    50Good ← edge
    51Moderate ← edge
    100Moderate
    101Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups
    300Very Unhealthy
    301Hazardous
    -5Invalid
    600Invalid

    A test table for the Air Quality Program. Nine runs, nine known answers.

    Two more habits: show variables on stage while testing so you see the box change; and use wait or slow mode to watch a loop tick. When output is wrong, ask “which variable is wrong, and which block changed it?” — that is debugging by tracing, from Unit 2.

    ExtraBeyond the basics: where the symbols came from

    The word algorithm comes from al-Khwarizmi, a Persian mathematician working in Baghdad around the year 820, whose book on calculating with Hindu-Arabic numerals spread the digits 0–9 to Europe. The = sign was invented in 1557 by the Welsh doctor Robert Recorde, who was tired of writing “is equal to”. And the first published computer program — a table of steps for Charles Babbage’s Analytical Engine to compute Bernoulli numbers — was written by Ada Lovelace in 1843, a century before any computer was built. Variables, loops and arithmetic: she had them all on paper.

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Trace this program by hand. What does it say? Then explain what would change if “set total to 0” were missing and last run left total = 10.

    set total ▾ to 0
    repeat 3
    change total ▾ by 4
    change total ▾ by -2
    say total

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Write total after every block: 0 → 4 → 8 → 12 → ?
    2. change by −2 subtracts.
    3. Without the set block, the loop starts from the OLD value.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: 0 → 4 → 8 → 12 → 10, so it says 10. Without set total to 0, it would start at 10: 10 → 14 → 18 → 22 → 20 — the program gives a different answer every time you run it. Always reset totals and counters first.
    Example 2

    Write the blocks for a program that asks for an AQI number and says “Good” (0–50), “Moderate” (51–100) or “Unhealthy” (101 or more). Then test it with 50, 51 and 100 by hand.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Ask → set aqi to answer.
    2. Chain if/else from the smallest range: aqi < 51 → Good.
    3. Inside the else: aqi < 101 → Moderate, else Unhealthy.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer:
    when 🏁 clicked
    ask AQI? and wait
    set aqi ▾ to answer
    if aqi < 51 then
    say Good
    else
    if aqi < 101 then
    say Moderate
    else
    say Unhealthy
    Trace: 50 < 51 → Good ✓. 51 < 51? no → 51 < 101 → Moderate ✓. 100 < 101 → Moderate ✓. 101 → neither → Unhealthy ✓. Using “< 51” instead of “< 50” is what makes 50 land in Good.
    Example 3

    A shop sells notebooks at 12 000 ₫ each. Write a program that asks how many notebooks, then says the total price like “Total: 60000”. Then change it so it also says how much change you get from 100 000 ₫.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. ask → set n to answer.
    2. total = n × 12000. Output needs join.
    3. change = 100000 − total.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer:
    when 🏁 clicked
    ask How many notebooks? and wait
    set n ▾ to answer
    set total ▾ to n × 12000
    say join Total: total for 2 seconds
    say join Change: 100000 − total
    For n = 5: total 60000, change 40000. Extra thinking: what if n = 9? Change would be −8000 — a good program adds if total > 100000 then say “Not enough money”.

    Practice

    Theory

    1What is a network?

    A network is two or more devices connected so they can share: a file, a printer, an internet connection, a message. Your home network is a LAN (Local Area Network) — everything inside one building. Your school has a bigger LAN with hundreds of devices. Networks in different places joined together make a WAN (Wide Area Network). The biggest WAN of all is the Internet: millions of networks around the world, all agreeing to speak the same language so any device can reach any other.

    A typical home LAN. In the Lab you will build this exactly, cable by cable.

    Why network at all? Without one, a photo on your tablet can only leave by USB stick (Unit 1). With one, the same photo reaches the printer in the next room, Grandma’s phone in Da Nang, and a cloud server in Singapore in seconds. Networks turn separate machines into a team.

    2Network devices: who does what

    Each box in a network has a job. A switch joins devices in one LAN with cables — it passes data only to the device it is meant for. An access point (Wi-Fi point) does the same job without wires. A router is the door between your LAN and other networks — it decides where data should go next and connects you to your ISP (internet service provider, e.g. Viettel, VNPT, FPT). At home, one box often contains router + switch + access point together. A server is a powerful computer that stores things for others: web pages, emails, game worlds, your class photos in Google Drive.

    DeviceJobRemember it as…
    Switch 🔀joins wired devices inside ONE networka smart multi-plug
    Access point 📶joins wireless (Wi-Fi) devices to the same networka switch without wires
    Router 📡connects your network to other networks; chooses the routethe front door + signpost
    Server 🖥️stores and serves data to many clientsthe librarian
    Client 💻📱a device that uses the networkthe reader
    Sensor 🌡️measures and sends readingsa tiny reporter

    Six kinds of box. The Lab’s network builder uses exactly these icons.

    Devices that use the network are clients: laptops, phones, tablets, printers, smart TVs, and increasingly tiny sensors — a temperature sensor in a greenhouse, a GPS tag on a dolphin. A sensor that sends its readings over a network is part of the Internet of Things.

    3Wired and wireless

    Data travels either along a cable (copper Ethernet, or glass fibre optic carrying light pulses) or through the air as radio waves — wireless. Cables are faster and never drop, but you cannot walk around with them. Wireless is convenient but weaker through walls and shared with everyone nearby. There is not one “wireless”: Wi-Fi covers a house, Bluetooth a room, mobile data (4G/5G) a city through cell towers, and satellites reach ships, planes and animals in the ocean where no tower exists.

    TechnologyReachNeedsUsed for
    Cable (Ethernet)up to 100 ma plug into a switchdesktop PCs, printers, servers — fastest and most reliable
    Wi-Fia house (~30 m)an access point + passwordlaptops, phones, tablets indoors
    Bluetootha room (~10 m)two paired devicesheadphones, speakers, smartwatch
    Mobile (4G/5G)a citya SIM + cell towersphones outdoors, cars, buses
    Satellitethe whole planetan antenna with a view of the skyships, planes, dolphin trackers

    Five ways for data to move. Reach grows down the table; speed and reliability shrink.

    Choosing is the same “size and distance” thinking as Unit 1: a printer that never moves → cable; a tablet on the sofa → Wi-Fi; a dolphin 200 km out at sea → satellite. Under the oceans, giant undersea cables carry about 99% of all international internet traffic — satellites carry only the last bit to places cables cannot reach.

    4How data travels: packets and addresses

    A network does not send a whole photo in one piece. It chops the data into small packets, gives each one a number and the address of the destination, and sends them off. Every device on a network has an address — an IP address looks like 192.168.1.12 — the way every house has a street number. Routers read the address on each packet and pass it toward its destination, choosing the best road at that moment. Packets from one message may take different roads; at the other end they are put back in order using their numbers, and if one is missing the receiver asks for it again.

    Three packets, three roads, one message. The Lab’s “send packet” animation shows this on your own network.

    This is why the internet keeps working when a cable breaks: routers simply choose another road. In the Lab you can cut a link and watch a packet find a new path — or fail, if there is no other path. A network with only one road to the outside has a single point of failure; good designs add a second link.

    5Communicating over networks — and tracking dolphins

    Every message app is a network program: email (a letter that waits on a server until you read it), messaging (Zalo, Messenger — near-instant, through the company’s servers), video calls (thousands of packets a second, both ways, so any delay is noticeable), and file sharing through the cloud (Unit 1). Machines communicate too: a sensor sends a tiny packet every minute; a server collects millions of them; a scientist’s laptop asks the server for a chart.

    HopFrom → toLinkWhy
    1Tag on dolphin → satelliteSatelliteno towers or cables at sea
    2Satellite → ground stationSatellitethe station has a big antenna
    3Ground station router → internet → centre’s routerFibre cablefast, reliable, long distance
    4Centre’s router → switch → serverEthernet cablethe server never moves
    5Access point → researchers’ tabletsWi-Fipeople walk around the centre

    Five hops from a dolphin’s fin to a scientist’s screen. Lab task 3 builds this network.

    Your unit project is a Dolphin Tracking Center. Marine scientists attach a small satellite tag to a dolphin’s fin. Each time the dolphin surfaces, the tag sends its GPS position and water temperature up to a satellite; the satellite relays it to a ground station; the station’s router sends it over the internet to the research centre’s server; researchers on tablets see the dolphin’s track on a map. Design task: which devices, which links (satellite, cable, Wi-Fi), and what happens if one link breaks?

    6Keeping a network safe

    Because networks share, they must also protect. Your home Wi-Fi needs a password so neighbours cannot use it or see your devices. Websites that show a padlock (https) scramble your packets so nobody along the road can read them — always look for it before typing a password. Public Wi-Fi (café, airport) is shared with strangers: fine for looking things up, not for logging in to anything important. And the SMART rules from Unit 1 apply to every message app.

    ExtraBeyond the basics: how the internet began

    The first message on the internet’s ancestor, ARPANET, was sent on 29 October 1969 between two universities in California. The student typed “LOGIN” — and the network crashed after “LO”. Two letters, and the internet had begun. Today about 5.5 billion people are online, roughly 600 undersea cables link the continents, and more than 18 billion “things” — sensors, cameras, dolphin tags — are connected too. In Vietnam about 79% of people use the internet. Every one of those connections still works the way this unit describes: packets, addresses, routers.

    Worked examples

    Example 1

    Nam’s family has a laptop, a phone, a tablet and a printer. The printer sits next to the router; everyone else moves around. Draw (in words) the home network: which devices use a cable, which use Wi-Fi, and what does the router connect to?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Things that never move → cable.
    2. Things you carry → Wi-Fi via the access point.
    3. The router’s other side goes to…?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: printer → cable → switch (or a port on the router box). Laptop, phone, tablet → Wi-Fi → access point → router. Router → the ISP’s line (fibre) → Internet. A cable for the printer means it never drops off the network; Wi-Fi for the rest because they move. If the laptop is used at a desk for video calls, a cable would give a smoother call.
    Example 2

    You send a 3 MB photo to a friend. Explain what happens to it between your phone and hers, using the words packet, address, router and reassemble.

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. 3 MB is far bigger than one packet (about 1 500 bytes).
    2. Each packet carries the destination address.
    3. What does the receiving phone do with 2 000 packets?
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: the phone chops the photo into about 2 000 numbered packets, each labelled with the friend’s (server’s) address. They go by Wi-Fi to your router, then hop from router to router across the ISP and the internet — different packets may take different roads. The messaging server stores them and forwards them to your friend’s phone, which reassembles them in number order; any missing packet is requested again. She sees one complete photo about a second later.
    Example 3

    The Dolphin Tracking Center loses its fibre cable in a storm. Which part of the dolphin’s data path stops working, and how would you design the centre so tracking continues?

    ▸Show hintHide hint
    1. Trace the five hops. Which one uses the fibre cable?
    2. Do the tags stop sending? Does the ground station stop receiving?
    3. Single point of failure → add a second road.
    ▸Show answerHide answer
    Answer: hop 3 (ground station → internet → centre) breaks. The tags still send and the ground station still receives, but the centre’s server gets nothing, so the researchers’ map freezes. Fix: give the centre a second link — a 4G/5G mobile router or its own satellite dish — so the router switches roads automatically when the fibre fails. Also have the ground station store readings while the link is down and send them when it returns, so no data is lost.

    A complete AQI program: (1) set a variable aqi from the answer; (2) all six official levels: 0–50 Good, 51–100 Moderate, 101–150 Unhealthy for sensitive groups, 151–200 Unhealthy, 201–300 Very unhealthy, 301+ Hazardous — one message each; (3) ALSO tell the player how many points above 50 the air is (aqi − 50) when it is not Good; (4) reject numbers below 0 with “That is not a valid AQI”.

    3. For every level except Good, say join “Above 50 by ” (aqi − 50).
    4. Test: −5, 30, 75, 120, 180, 250, 400.
