    Real Scratch. The Lab tab is for quick, auto-checked drills; this tab uses MIT’s official Scratch 3 — the tool the school uses for the Yes/No Quiz project. Work through it in order: Setup → Tutorial → Model projects → Exercises → Competition.

    Which Scratch should we use?

    There are three ways to run the real Scratch 3, and all of them are free. 1 · Online at scratch.mit.edu/projects/editor — works in Chrome, Edge, Safari or Firefox, and you do not need an account to create and save projects to your computer. 2 · Scratch Desktop app (offline, no internet needed once installed): download from scratch.mit.edu/download — Windows 10+, macOS, ChromeOS and Android; on a Mac it is also in the App Store. No login required. 3 · iPad: there is no Scratch 3 iPad app (the “ScratchJr” app is a different, simpler program for ages 5–7); open Safari and go to scratch.mit.edu instead — tablets are supported, phones are not.

    Vietnamese menus: click the 🌐 globe icon at the top-left of the editor and choose Tiếng Việt. Every block is translated (e.g. hỏi … và đợi, nếu … thì). In this guide we show the English names first, because that is what the school uses, with the Vietnamese name in brackets.

    Saving: menu File → Save to your computer creates a .sb3 file (name it e.g. YesNoQuiz.sb3). Next time use File → Load from your computer. Without an account there is no automatic saving — save before closing!

    A map of the Scratch editor

    A · Block palette — the 9 colour groups on the far left (Motion, Looks, Sound, Events, Control, Sensing, Operators, Variables, My Blocks) and the blocks of the chosen group next to them. B · Code area — drag blocks here and snap them together. C · Stage — where the sprite acts; the green flag ▶ starts, the red sign ⏹ stops. D · Sprite list — every character in the project; click one to edit its code. The stage (backdrops) is the small box on the right. Our Lab tab is a miniature of A + B + C.

    The blocks this unit uses

    Only eleven blocks are needed for everything in Unit 2. Learn their exact names and colours — in a test you must find them fast.

    Block (English)Tiếng Việt trong ScratchGroupWhat it does
    when green flag clickedKhi bấm vào 🏁EventsStarts the program
    when [space] key pressedkhi bấm phím [space]EventsStarts when a key is pressed
    ask [ ] and waithỏi [ ] và đợiSensingShows a question and a text box
    answertrả lờiSensingWhat the player typed
    if < > thennếu < > thìControlRuns the inside only when true
    if < > then / elsenếu < > thì / nếu không thìControlTwo doors: true → top, false → bottom
    ( ) = ( ), ( ) > ( ), ( ) < ( )( ) = ( ), ( ) > ( ), ( ) < ( )OperatorsCompare, report true/false
    join ( ) ( )kết hợp ( ) ( )OperatorsGlues two texts together
    say ( ) for ( ) secondsnói ( ) trong ( ) giâyLooksSpeech bubble
    set [score] to ( )đặt [score] thành ( )VariablesStore a value in a variable
    change [score] by ( )thay đổi [score] một lượng ( )VariablesAdd to a variable

    Three habits that save you from bugs

    1 · One hat block per script. Every script starts with a yellow hat (when 🏁 clicked). A stack with no hat never runs. 2 · Look at the shape. Pointed hexagon blocks (=, >, <) only fit the pointed hole of IF; round blocks (answer, join) only fit round holes. If it will not drop in, it is the wrong shape. 3 · Test both doors. After building an if/else, run it twice — once with an answer that makes the condition true, once with one that makes it false.

    Open Scratch, keep this page next to it, and build each lesson exactly as shown. The “You should see” line tells you what a correct result looks like.

    Lesson 1 · Ask, answer, join

    1. 1

      Click Events (yellow). Drag when 🏁 clicked into the code area.

    2. 2

      Click Sensing (light blue). Drag ask … and wait under the hat. Click the white oval and type What is your name?

    3. 3

      Click Looks (purple). Drag say … for 2 seconds underneath.

    4. 4

      Click Operators (green). Drag join apple banana and drop it INTO the white oval of the say block (the oval lights up when you are over it).

    5. 5

      Change apple to Hello, (with a space). From Sensing drag the round answer block into the second slot, replacing banana.

    6. 6

      Press 🏁. Type your name in the box at the bottom of the stage and press Enter.

      when 🏁 clicked
      ask What is your name? and wait
      say join Hello, answer for 2 seconds

    You should see: the cat asks the question, then says “Hello, Nyna!” for 2 seconds. Why it works: answer is a box that remembers whatever was typed last; join glues the greeting and the box together into one sentence.

    Lesson 2 · Your first binary decision (if / else)

    1. 1

      Start a new script: when 🏁 clicked → ask Do you like pizza? and wait.

    2. 2

      Click Control (orange). Find the block with TWO mouths: if < > then … else. Drag it under the ask block.

    3. 3

      Click Operators. Drag the pointed ( ) = (50) block into the pointed hole of the IF.

    4. 4

      From Sensing drop answer into the LEFT slot of =. Click the RIGHT slot, delete 50 and type yes.

    5. 5

      Put say Me too! for 2 seconds in the top mouth and say Oh, really? for 2 seconds in the else mouth.

    6. 6

      Run it twice: type yes, then run again and type no.

      when 🏁 clicked
      ask Do you like pizza? and wait
      if answer = yes then
      say Me too! for 2 seconds
      else
      say Oh, really? for 2 seconds

    You should see: “Me too!” for yes and “Oh, really?” for anything else — never both. Why: the condition answer = yes is checked ONCE, right when the program reaches the IF. True opens the top door, false opens the bottom door. Try typing YES — Scratch ignores capital letters, so it still counts as yes. Try yes! — the “!” breaks the match.

    Lesson 3 · Numbers as answers

    1. 1

      Build the same shape as Lesson 2, but ask How many legs does a spider have? and compare answer = 8.

    2. 2

      In the else mouth, use join so the cat repeats the wrong number: join (No — a spider has 8 legs, not ) (answer).

      when 🏁 clicked
      ask How many legs does a spider have? and wait
      if answer = 8 then
      say Correct! 🕷 for 2 seconds
      else
      say join No — a spider has 8 legs, not answer for 3 seconds
    3. 3

      Test with 8, then with 6, then with eight (a word!). What happens with the word?

    You should see: 8 → Correct; 6 → “No — a spider has 8 legs, not 6”; “eight” → also wrong, because Scratch compares the characters e-i-g-h-t with 8. If you want both to count, you need or: answer = 8 or answer = eight (see Lesson 5).

    Lesson 4 · Greater than, less than, and the third case

    1. 1

      Ask Type a number. Use if answer > 10 then say Bigger than 10 else ….

    2. 2

      Inside the else mouth, put ANOTHER if/else: if answer < 10 then say Smaller than 10 else say Exactly 10!. An IF inside an IF is called nesting.

      when 🏁 clicked
      ask Type a number and wait
      if answer > 10 then
      say Bigger than 10 for 2 seconds
      else
      if answer < 10 then
      say Smaller than 10 for 2 seconds
      else
      say Exactly 10! for 2 seconds
    3. 3

      Test with 25, 3 and 10.

    You should see three different replies. Why we need the third door: > 10 is false for 10 itself, and so is < 10 — the number 10 falls through both, so the innermost else catches “exactly 10”. Trace it with your finger: 10 → first condition false → second condition false → “Exactly 10!”.

    Lesson 5 · Keeping score with a variable (and “or”)

    1. 1

      Click Variables (orange) → Make a Variable → name it score → OK. A checkbox next to it shows the score on the stage.

    2. 2

      Right after the hat block put set score to 0 — every game must start from zero.

    3. 3

      Ask Is a tomato a fruit?. Condition: (answer = yes) or (answer = y) — drag the green or block into the IF hole first, then drop one = block into each of its two holes.

    4. 4

      THEN mouth: change score by 1 + say Correct! for 1 seconds. ELSE mouth: say Wrong — it is a fruit! for 2 seconds.

    5. 5

      After the IF: say join (Score: ) (score) for 2 seconds — drag the orange round score block into join.

      when 🏁 clicked
      set score ▾ to 0
      ask Is a tomato a fruit? and wait
      if answer = yes or answer = y then
      change score ▾ by 1
      say Correct! for 1 seconds
      else
      say Wrong — it is a fruit! for 2 seconds
      say join Score: score for 2 seconds

    You should see the score box on the stage change from 0 to 1 when you answer yes or y. Why “set to 0” matters: without it, the score from the last run is still in the box, so the second game would start at 1. This is the most common bug in quiz projects.

    Three complete projects. Build them exactly, run them, then change one thing at a time (a question, a reply, a sound) and watch what happens. Every project is explained block by block.

    Model 1 · Yes/No Quiz — the unit project

    Purpose: a 3-question quiz that replies to every answer and shows the final score. Expected outcome: the player answers three yes/no questions, hears a sound for right and wrong, and sees “Your score: n / 3”; a perfect score gets a special message.

    when 🏁 clicked
    switch backdrop to Blue Sky ▾
    set score ▾ to 0
    say Yes/No Quiz! Answer yes or no. for 2 seconds
    ask Is the Sun a star? and wait
    if answer = yes then
    change score ▾ by 1
    start sound Collect ▾
    say Correct! ✅ for 1 seconds
    else
    start sound Buzz ▾
    say Wrong — the Sun IS a star. for 2 seconds
    ask Is a spider an insect? and wait
    if answer = no then
    change score ▾ by 1
    start sound Collect ▾
    say Correct! ✅ for 1 seconds
    else
    start sound Buzz ▾
    say Wrong — spiders have 8 legs, insects have 6. for 2 seconds
    ask Is Hanoi the capital of Vietnam? and wait
    if answer = yes then
    change score ▾ by 1
    start sound Collect ▾
    say Correct! ✅ for 1 seconds
    else
    start sound Buzz ▾
    say Wrong — Hanoi is the capital. for 2 seconds
    if score = 3 then
    switch costume to costume2 ▾
    say Perfect score! 🏆 for 3 seconds
    else
    say join Your score: join score / 3 for 3 seconds
    • switch backdrop to Blue Sky — click the Stage (bottom right) → Backdrops tab → choose a backdrop from the library first, then this block can pick it.
    • set score to 0 comes BEFORE the first question — resetting is the first thing every game does.
    • Each question is the same 3-block pattern: ask → if/else → feedback. Once one works, right-click it → Duplicate and just change the question and the correct word.
    • start sound Collect / Buzz: Sounds tab → choose sounds from the library. Sound makes right/wrong obvious without reading.
    • The last if/else compares the VARIABLE, not the answer: score = 3. join inside join builds “Your score: 2 / 3”.
    • Evaluation checklist: ☐ asks 3 questions ☐ replies to right AND wrong ☐ score starts at 0 ☐ score shown at the end ☐ works when I type YES in capitals.

    Model 2 · The password door

    Purpose: only the right password lets the sprite through. Shows that a decision can control MOVEMENT, not just speech.

    when 🏁 clicked
    set tries ▾ to 0
    go to x: -150 y: 0
    ask Password? and wait
    if answer = open123 then
    say Welcome! for 1 seconds
    glide 2 secs to x: 150 y: 0
    start sound Magic Spell ▾
    else
    change tries ▾ by 1
    say join Wrong password. Tries: tries for 2 seconds
    • go to x: −150 y: 0 puts the sprite on the left every run (left is negative x).
    • glide 2 secs to x: 150 y: 0 (Motion) moves smoothly across the stage — much nicer than move for “walking through the door”.
    • tries counts wrong attempts. Extension: wrap the ask + if/else in repeat until answer = open123 so the door keeps asking, and add if tries = 3 then say Locked! stop all.

    Model 3 · Guess my number (comparison + loop)

    Purpose: the computer picks a secret number; the player guesses; every guess gets a hint “too big / too small”. This joins Unit 2 (selection) with what you learned about loops.

    when 🏁 clicked
    set secret ▾ to pick random 1 to 20
    set guesses ▾ to 0
    say I am thinking of a number from 1 to 20. for 2 seconds
    repeat until answer = secret
    ask Your guess? and wait
    change guesses ▾ by 1
    if answer > secret then
    say Too big! ⬇ for 1 seconds
    else
    if answer < secret then
    say Too small! ⬆ for 1 seconds
    say join Yes! You found it in join guesses guesses. for 3 seconds
    • pick random 1 to 20 (Operators) gives a different secret each game. Store it in a variable, or every comparison would pick a NEW random number!
    • repeat until answer = secret keeps asking until the guess is right. Inside, we do NOT need an “equal” branch — equality ends the loop by itself.
    • The nested if > … else if < is exactly Lesson 4 with a variable instead of the number 10.
    • Trace it: secret = 7, guesses 10 → “Too big”, 3 → “Too small”, 7 → loop ends → “found it in 3 guesses”.

    Ten exercises from ★ (copy a pattern) to ★★★★ (design it yourself). Do them in order. Always try for at least 5 minutes before opening the solution — the struggle is where the learning happens. Each solution is one correct way; yours may differ and still be right if it passes the tests.

    1

    Favourite colour

    ★☆☆☆

    Ask “What is your favourite colour?”. If the answer is blue, say “Like the sky!”; otherwise say “Nice choice!”.

    InputOutput
    blueLike the sky!
    BlueLike the sky! (capitals ignored)
    redNice choice!
    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    Same shape as Lesson 2 — only the words change.

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án
    when 🏁 clicked
    ask What is your favourite colour? and wait
    if answer = blue then
    say Like the sky! for 2 seconds
    else
    say Nice choice! for 2 seconds
    • One ask, one if/else, one = block comparing answer with the word.
    2

    Old enough?

    ★☆☆☆

    Ask “How old are you?”. If the answer is greater than 9, say “You can join the Year 5 club!”, else say “Not yet — soon!”.

    InputOutput
    10You can join…
    9Not yet — soon!
    7Not yet — soon!
    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    Use the > block. Which side does answer go on?

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án
    when 🏁 clicked
    ask How old are you? and wait
    if answer > 9 then
    say You can join the Year 5 club! for 2 seconds
    else
    say Not yet — soon! for 2 seconds
    • answer > 9: true for 10, 11, 12…; false for 9 and below. Test with exactly 9 — it must say “Not yet”.
    3

    Even or odd

    ★★☆☆

    Ask for a number and say whether it is EVEN or ODD.

    InputOutput
    88 is EVEN
    1515 is ODD
    00 is EVEN
    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    A number is even when dividing by 2 leaves no remainder. Look in Operators for a block with the word mod — it gives the remainder.

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án
    when 🏁 clicked
    ask Type a number and wait
    if answer mod 2 = 0 then
    say join answer is EVEN for 2 seconds
    else
    say join answer is ODD for 2 seconds
    • answer mod 2 is 0 for even numbers and 1 for odd numbers. The = block compares that with 0.
    • Drop the mod block into the LEFT slot of =, then answer into the left slot of mod. Three blocks nested — take it slowly.
    4

    Traffic light

    ★★☆☆

    Ask “What colour is the light?”. red → “Stop!”, green → “Go!”, anything else → “Get ready…”. Use nested if/else (an IF inside the else mouth).

    InputOutput
    redStop!
    greenGo!
    yellowGet ready…
    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    First decide red / not red. Inside “not red”, decide green / not green.

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án
    when 🏁 clicked
    ask What colour is the light? and wait
    if answer = red then
    say Stop! for 2 seconds
    else
    if answer = green then
    say Go! for 2 seconds
    else
    say Get ready… for 2 seconds
    • Three outcomes need TWO binary decisions. The first IF splits red from the rest; the second IF, living in the else mouth, splits green from the rest.
    • Trace “yellow”: red? no → green? no → “Get ready…”.
    5

    Bigger of two

    ★★☆☆

    Ask for two numbers (two ask blocks). Say which one is bigger, or “They are equal”. Hint: answer only remembers the LAST thing typed.

    InputOutput
    7, 37 is bigger
    2, 99 is bigger
    4, 4They are equal
    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    After the first ask, immediately do set a to answer to keep it. Then ask again and store in b.

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án
    when 🏁 clicked
    ask First number? and wait
    set a ▾ to answer
    ask Second number? and wait
    set b ▾ to answer
    if a > b then
    say join a is bigger for 2 seconds
    else
    if a < b then
    say join b is bigger for 2 seconds
    else
    say They are equal for 2 seconds
    • set a to (answer) right after the first ask, set b to (answer) right after the second. Variables a and b are the “boxes” that keep both numbers.
    • This is the first time you compare two VARIABLES instead of answer and a number. Same pointed blocks, different contents.
    6

    Password with three tries

    ★★★☆

    The password is xu2016. Let the player try up to 3 times. Correct → “Welcome!” and stop asking. After 3 wrong tries → “Locked!”.

    InputOutput
    xu2016Welcome! (stops)
    abc, xu2016Wrong!, Welcome!
    a, b, cWrong! ×3, Locked!
    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    Use repeat 3 around ask + if. To leave the loop early when correct, use stop this script (Control) after Welcome.

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án
    when 🏁 clicked
    repeat 3
    ask Password? and wait
    if answer = xu2016 then
    say Welcome! for 2 seconds
    stop this script ▾
    else
    say Wrong! for 1 seconds
    say Locked! for 2 seconds
    • repeat 3 gives three chances. Each time: ask, check.
    • stop this script ends everything — so “Locked!” (which is AFTER the loop) is only reached if all three tries were wrong.
    • Alternative: repeat until (answer = xu2016) or (tries = 3) with a tries variable — also correct.
    7

    Grade the score

    ★★★☆

    Ask for a test score from 0 to 10. 9 or 10 → “Excellent”; 7 or 8 → “Good”; 5 or 6 → “Pass”; below 5 → “Try again”. Also, if the number is bigger than 10 or smaller than 0, say “That is not a valid score”.

    InputOutput
    10Excellent
    7Good
    5Pass
    2Try again
    11That is not a valid score
    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    Check the invalid case FIRST with or. Then go from the top down: > 8 → Excellent, else > 6 → Good, else > 4 → Pass, else Try again.

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án
    when 🏁 clicked
    ask Score (0–10)? and wait
    if answer > 10 or answer < 0 then
    say That is not a valid score for 2 seconds
    else
    if answer > 8 then
    say Excellent for 2 seconds
    else
    if answer > 6 then
    say Good for 2 seconds
    else
    if answer > 4 then
    say Pass for 2 seconds
    else
    say Try again for 2 seconds
    • Order matters. Because we test > 8 first, a 9 never reaches the “Good” test. Going top-down with > means each branch only needs ONE comparison.
    • or joins two conditions: the score is invalid if EITHER is true.
    8

    Rock, paper, scissors

    ★★★☆

    The player types rock, paper or scissors. The computer picks one at random and says who wins. Rules: rock beats scissors, scissors beats paper, paper beats rock.

    InputOutput
    rock (cpu: scissors)You win!
    paper (cpu: paper)Draw!
    scissors (cpu: rock)I win!
    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    Store the computer’s choice: set cpu to pick random 1 to 3, then turn 1/2/3 into a word with three IFs. Compare words: same → draw; then list the three winning pairs with and.

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án
    when 🏁 clicked
    ask rock, paper or scissors? and wait
    set me ▾ to answer
    set n ▾ to pick random 1 to 3
    if n = 1 then
    set cpu ▾ to rock
    if n = 2 then
    set cpu ▾ to paper
    if n = 3 then
    set cpu ▾ to scissors
    say join I chose cpu for 1 seconds
    if me = cpu then
    say Draw! for 2 seconds
    else
    if me = rock and cpu = scissors or me = scissors and cpu = paper or me = paper and cpu = rock then
    say You win! 🎉 for 2 seconds
    else
    say I win! 🤖 for 2 seconds
    • set me to (answer) right after ask — again, keep the answer before anything else changes it.
    • The big condition reads: (me=rock AND cpu=scissors) OR (me=scissors AND cpu=paper) OR (me=paper AND cpu=rock). Build it from the inside out: three and blocks first, then join them with two or blocks.
    • If it is not a draw and not a win, it must be a loss — that is why the last else needs no condition.
    9

    Times-table quiz with random questions

    ★★★★

    Ask 5 random multiplication questions (numbers 2–9). Keep score. At the end say the score AND a comment: 5 → “Maths star!”, 3–4 → “Well done”, less → “Keep practising”.

    InputOutput
    all 5 right5/5 — Maths star!
    3 right3/5 — Well done
    1 right1/5 — Keep practising
    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    Inside repeat 5: pick a and b at random, ask join (join a ( × )) b, then if answer = a × b. After the loop, a nested if/else on score.

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án
    when 🏁 clicked
    set score ▾ to 0
    repeat 5
    set a ▾ to pick random 2 to 9
    set b ▾ to pick random 2 to 9
    ask join join a × join b = ? and wait
    if answer = a × b then
    change score ▾ by 1
    say ✔ for 1 seconds
    else
    say join ✘ It was a × b for 2 seconds
    if score = 5 then
    say 5/5 — Maths star! for 3 seconds
    else
    if score > 2 then
    say join score /5 — Well done for 3 seconds
    else
    say join score /5 — Keep practising for 3 seconds
    • The question text is built with join-inside-join: a, “ × ”, b, “ = ?”. join only takes two things, so nest it.
    • The correct answer is computed by the green a × b block, dropped straight into the right slot of =.
    • score > 2 means 3 or 4 here, because 5 was already caught by the first test.
    10

    Design your own: the sorting hat

    ★★★★

    Design a program that asks THREE yes/no questions about the player (e.g. “Do you like animals?”, “Are you brave?”, “Do you like reading?”) and uses a variable to put them into one of three teams. Write the purpose and the expected outcome first, then a checklist of criteria, then build it. There is no single right answer — your solution passes if it meets your own criteria.

    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    One idea: a variable points; each yes adds a different amount (1, 2, 4). Then 0–1 → Team Owl, 2–4 → Team Fox, 5–7 → Team Lion.

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án
    when 🏁 clicked
    set points ▾ to 0
    ask Do you like animals? and wait
    if answer = yes then
    change points ▾ by 1
    ask Are you brave? and wait
    if answer = yes then
    change points ▾ by 2
    ask Do you like reading? and wait
    if answer = yes then
    change points ▾ by 4
    if points < 2 then
    say Team Owl 🦉 for 3 seconds
    else
    if points < 5 then
    say Team Fox 🦊 for 3 seconds
    else
    say Team Lion 🦁 for 3 seconds
    • Here plain if … then (one door) is enough for each question — a “no” simply adds nothing.
    • Sample criteria: ☐ three questions ☐ every answer affects the result ☐ exactly one team is announced ☐ a friend tested it and got a sensible team.
    • Evaluate against your list, then improve one thing: a backdrop per team, a sound, or a fourth question.

    The competition: Hội thi Tin học trẻ toàn quốc — Bảng A (Primary)

    Vietnam’s biggest school computing contest, run every year by the Youth Union’s CYTAST centre (tinhoctre.vn). Bảng A is for primary pupils (grades 1–5). The 2026 rules say contestants program in Scratch or Python; the online qualifying rounds (March–April) are 90–100 minutes with about 5 problems, each worth 100 points, graded automatically by comparing your program’s output with the expected output; regional rounds are in July and the national final in August. Provincial and district rounds (cấp tỉnh / quận) are held earlier and often include Scratch drawing and game tasks graded by hand from the .sb3 file.

    What the problems look like: short maths-style tasks — read some numbers, compute, print a result — exactly the ask → compute → say pattern of this unit, plus loops. Reading the problem carefully is half the score: the examples show the exact output format. Below are six real problems from 2024–2025 provincial rounds that use selection, each with a full Scratch solution.

    How to practise for it: a big archive of past papers (over 80 pages) is at scratch.hourofcode.vn — Thư viện đề thi; the 2026 free-entry qualifying paper is at this page (5 problems: rectangle area, times table, colouring the schoolyard, clock, grouping). Internationally, the International Scratch Creative Programming Olympiad has a “My Book” category for ages 9–10: a voiced animated story retelling a book — a different, creative style of contest.

    Contest habits that score points: (1) use one ask per input, in the order the problem lists them, and store each in a variable immediately; (2) print EXACTLY the text the examples show — no extra words, no missing spaces; (3) test with every example in the problem before moving on; (4) numbers can be huge (up to 109) — never loop up to the number itself when a formula exists.

    1

    Độ dài (Length) — Tiên Du, Bắc Ninh 2025, Bài 1

    Tin học trẻ Bảng A, huyện Tiên Du, Bắc Ninh 2025 ↗

    1 cm = 10 mm. A ruler is a cm and b mm long. How many mm is that? Input: a, b (1 ≤ a, b ≤ 1000). Output: the length in mm.

    InputOutput
    2 525
    12 40160
    ▸How to think about it · Cách suy nghĩHide the approach · Ẩn cách suy nghĩ

    No decision needed — this is the warm-up that teaches the input/output pattern: two asks, one formula, one say.

    ▸Full Scratch solution · Lời giải Scratch đầy đủFull Scratch solution · Lời giải Scratch đầy đủ
    when 🏁 clicked
    ask a and wait
    set a ▾ to answer
    ask b and wait
    set b ▾ to answer
    say a × 10 + b
    • Formula: a × 10 + b. The say block prints just the number — the graders compare it to “25”.
    • Each set … to (answer) saves the number the moment it is typed, because the next ask will overwrite answer.
    2

    Chia nhóm (Grouping) — Tiên Du, Bắc Ninh 2025, Bài 2

    Tin học trẻ Bảng A, huyện Tiên Du, Bắc Ninh 2025 ↗

    100 pupils take part in a contest and must be split into groups of at most x pupils. What is the smallest number of groups? Input: x (1 ≤ x ≤ 100).

    InputOutput
    602
    254
    304
    ▸How to think about it · Cách suy nghĩHide the approach · Ẩn cách suy nghĩ

    Divide 100 by x. If it divides exactly, that is the answer; if there is a remainder, one more group is needed for the leftover pupils. That “if there is a remainder” is a binary decision — use mod.

    ▸Full Scratch solution · Lời giải Scratch đầy đủFull Scratch solution · Lời giải Scratch đầy đủ
    when 🏁 clicked
    ask x and wait
    set x ▾ to answer
    set g ▾ to floor ▾ of 100 ÷ x
    if 100 mod x > 0 then
    change g ▾ by 1
    say g
    • floor of (100 ÷ x) is the Operators block “[abs] of ( )” with the menu set to floor — it rounds DOWN (100 ÷ 30 = 3.33 → 3).
    • if 100 mod x > 0 then change g by 1: the leftover pupils need one extra group. 30 → 3 full groups + 10 left → 4.
    • Shortcut used by experts: ceiling of (100 ÷ x) does both steps at once. Both are accepted.
    3

    Tổng các số lẻ (Sum of odd numbers) — Hậu Giang 2025, Bài 1

    Tin học trẻ Bảng A, tỉnh Hậu Giang 2025 ↗

    Compute the sum of the first n odd numbers. Input: n with 0 < n < 100. If n does not satisfy the condition, output “Khong thoa man de bai”.

    InputOutput
    39 (1 + 3 + 5)
    101Khong thoa man de bai
    ▸How to think about it · Cách suy nghĩHide the approach · Ẩn cách suy nghĩ

    Two parts: (1) a validity check with or — n ≤ 0 OR n ≥ 100 → the error message; (2) otherwise add up 1, 3, 5, … with a loop. Bonus: the sum of the first n odd numbers is always n × n (3 → 9, 4 → 16) — a one-block answer!

    ▸Full Scratch solution · Lời giải Scratch đầy đủFull Scratch solution · Lời giải Scratch đầy đủ
    when 🏁 clicked
    ask n and wait
    set n ▾ to answer
    if n < 1 or n > 99 then
    say Khong thoa man de bai
    else
    set sum ▾ to 0
    set k ▾ to 1
    repeat n
    change sum ▾ by k
    change k ▾ by 2
    say sum
    • The or condition mirrors the words “does not satisfy 0 < n < 100”. Write the failing cases, not the passing one — it is easier to get right.
    • repeat n with k jumping by 2 visits 1, 3, 5… — n numbers exactly. change sum by k adds each one.
    • The error text must be typed EXACTLY, without Vietnamese accents, as in the problem.
    4

    Số lớn nhất chia hết cho 3 và 7 — Hậu Giang 2025, Bài 3

    Tin học trẻ Bảng A, tỉnh Hậu Giang 2025 ↗

    Five different numbers are entered. Find the largest one that is divisible by BOTH 3 and 7.

    InputOutput
    7 3 21 42 1442
    ▸How to think about it · Cách suy nghĩHide the approach · Ẩn cách suy nghĩ

    Read the five numbers one at a time in a loop. For each: is it divisible by 3 AND by 7 (both remainders 0) AND bigger than the best so far? If yes, it becomes the new best. Three conditions joined by and.

    ▸Full Scratch solution · Lời giải Scratch đầy đủFull Scratch solution · Lời giải Scratch đầy đủ
    when 🏁 clicked
    set best ▾ to 0
    repeat 5
    ask number and wait
    if answer mod 3 = 0 and answer mod 7 = 0 and answer > best then
    set best ▾ to answer
    say best
    • “Divisible by 3” is answer mod 3 = 0. Divisible by both 3 and 7 is the same as divisible by 21 — you could also test answer mod 21 = 0.
    • best starts at 0 so the first valid number always replaces it. set best to (answer) remembers it.
    • This “keep the best so far” pattern appears in almost every contest.
    5

    Chia bi (Sharing marbles) — Long An 2025, Bài 2

    Tin học trẻ Bảng A, tỉnh Long An 2025 ↗

    Lan has N marbles, her little sister Hương has M. Every day Lan gives Hương 1 marble. After L days, what is the difference between their numbers of marbles? Output exactly: “Số bi chênh lệch của 2 chị em là: …”. (1 ≤ N, M, L ≤ 109)

    InputOutput
    8 5 2Số bi chênh lệch của 2 chị em là: 1
    2 3 3Số bi chênh lệch của 2 chị em là: 5
    ▸How to think about it · Cách suy nghĩHide the approach · Ẩn cách suy nghĩ

    After L days Lan has N − L and Hương has M + L. The difference could come out negative (example 2: 2−3 = −1 vs 3+3 = 6 → −7), and a difference is never negative — so IF it is below 0, flip its sign. L can be a billion, so compute with a formula, never a day-by-day loop.

    ▸Full Scratch solution · Lời giải Scratch đầy đủFull Scratch solution · Lời giải Scratch đầy đủ
    when 🏁 clicked
    ask N and wait
    set N ▾ to answer
    ask M and wait
    set M ▾ to answer
    ask L and wait
    set L ▾ to answer
    set d ▾ to N − L − M + L
    if d < 0 then
    set d ▾ to 0 − d
    say join Số bi chênh lệch của 2 chị em là: d
    • d = (N − L) − (M + L). Check example 1: (8−2) − (5+2) = 6 − 7 = −1 → flip → 1 ✔.
    • if d < 0 then set d to 0 − d is the “absolute value” decision. Scratch also has abs of ( ) in Operators — one block instead of an IF.
    • The output sentence must match letter for letter, including the colon and the space.
    6

    Vẽ hình theo phím (Draw a shape by key) — Thanh Xuân, Hà Nội 2024, Câu 1

    Tin học trẻ Bảng A, quận Thanh Xuân, Hà Nội 2024 ↗

    Write a program that draws a shape with side / radius 57 when a key is pressed: 3 → triangle, 4 → square, 5 → pentagon, 6 → hexagon, 8 → octagon, 0 → circle. (Save as Vehinh.sb3.)

    ▸How to think about it · Cách suy nghĩHide the approach · Ẩn cách suy nghĩ

    Here the decision is made by EVENTS instead of IF: one “when [3] key pressed” script per shape. All the polygons share one idea — repeat n times: move 57, turn 360 ÷ n. Use the Pen extension (bottom-left “Add Extension” button) for pen down.

    ▸Full Scratch solution · Lời giải Scratch đầy đủFull Scratch solution · Lời giải Scratch đầy đủ
    when 4 ▾ key pressed
    erase all
    pen down
    repeat 4
    move 57 steps
    turn ↻ 90 degrees
    pen up
    when 6 ▾ key pressed
    erase all
    pen down
    repeat 6
    move 57 steps
    turn ↻ 60 degrees
    pen up
    when 0 ▾ key pressed
    erase all
    pen down
    repeat 360
    move 1 steps
    turn ↻ 1 degrees
    pen up
    • Square: 4 × (move 57, turn 90). Hexagon: 6 × (move 57, turn 60). The turn is always 360 ÷ number of sides: triangle 120, pentagon 72, octagon 45.
    • A circle is a polygon with very many tiny sides: 360 × (move 1, turn 1). To get radius 57 exactly, use move 1 with turn 1 and a step of about 57 × 2 × 3.14 ÷ 360 ≈ 1 — good enough for graders.
    • erase all first, so pressing another key draws a fresh shape. Six hat blocks = six binary decisions made by the keyboard.

    Real tools: Canva. The Lab trains the skills (typing, sorting, planning); this tab builds the real unit project — an internet-safety video — in Canva, step by step.

    The tool: Canva (free for students)

    Your school makes the safety video in Canva — a website (canva.com) and app for posters, slides and videos. Canva for Education is 100% free for K-12 students when a teacher invites them; at home a parent can create a free personal account. It runs in Chrome/Safari on a laptop, and there is a Canva app for tablets.

    Where things are: the left panel holds Design (templates), Elements (shapes, icons, stickers, stock video), Text, Uploads (your photos), and Audio. The middle is your page. Videos have a timeline at the bottom — each page is one scene, and you set how many seconds it plays.

    Saving and sharing: Canva saves automatically to your account. To get a real video file: Share → Download → MP4 Video → Download. That .mp4 plays on any phone or laptop — that is the compatibility lesson in action.

    Build the video from the storyboard you made in the Lab. One scene = one Canva page.

    Step by step: your internet-safety video in Canva

    1. 1

      Go to canva.com → Create a design → Video. Name it “Internet Safety Tips”.

    2. 2

      Page 1 = Hello scene: Text → add a heading “5 Internet Safety Tips”; Elements → search “kids computer” and add an illustration.

    3. 3

      Press + Add page for each tip (SMART: Safe, Meet, Accepting, Reliable, Tell). Heading = the rule, smaller text = one sentence, one icon (search “lock”, “stranger”, “link”, “question”, “adult”).

    4. 4

      Set each page’s time: click the page in the timeline → the clock/duration → 8–12 seconds. Total 40–70 s.

    5. 5

      Add your voice: Uploads → Record yourself (or Audio → a calm background track). Add a transition between pages (click between two pages → Add transition → Dissolve).

    6. 6

      Preview (▶ Play). Fix anything too fast to read. Then Share → Download → MP4 Video. Check the .mp4 plays on a phone.

    Model video script — “5 Internet Safety Tips” (62 s)

    Purpose: teach classmates the SMART rules in about one minute. Expected outcome: a .mp4 with 6 scenes, readable text, a voice-over, that plays on the class TV.

    #SceneOn screenVoice-overs
    1HelloTitle + kid with laptop 🙋“Hi, I am Nyna. Here are five tips to stay safe online.”8
    2S — SafeLock icon 🔒, “Keep it private”“Never share your address, school or password.”12
    3M — MeetTwo avatars + adult 👪“Never meet an online friend without an adult.”12
    4A — AcceptingLink with ✘“Don’t open links or files from people you don’t know.”10
    5R + T — Reliable, Tell❓ + speech bubble 💬“Not everything online is true. If something worries you, tell a trusted adult.”14
    6Bye“Stay SMART!” ✅“Be smart, be kind, be safe. Bye!”6
    • Big text, few words: a viewer needs about 3 seconds per line to read it.
    • One idea per scene — that is the “sequence” you learned in algorithms, applied to storytelling.
    • Checklist before download: ☐ every SMART rule appears ☐ no personal info on screen ☐ voice matches text ☐ total under 90 s.

    Practice tasks on the real tools, easy to hard. Each has a model answer.

    1

    Name that file

    ★☆☆☆

    On your computer, find one picture, one video and one document. Write down each file’s full name including the extension and its size.

    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    Right-click → Properties (Windows) or Get Info (Mac). On a phone: the ⓘ button in Photos.

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án

    Example answer: birthday.jpg 3.2 MB · dance.mp4 148 MB · story.docx 24 KB. Notice the video is 40× bigger than the photo and 6 000× bigger than the document.

    • Sizes vary, but video is always the giant.
    2

    Export to a common format

    ★★☆☆

    Make a one-page poster in Canva (any topic) and download it twice: once as PNG and once as PDF. Open both on a different device (a phone). Which is bigger? Which looks sharper when you zoom?

    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    Share → Download → File type.

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án

    Both open everywhere (compatible formats). The PDF usually stays sharp when zoomed because text is stored as text; the PNG is a picture of pixels and blurs when enlarged. PNG is better for a picture to post; PDF for printing or documents.

    • This is the “choose the format for the job” skill.
    3

    Move a file three ways

    ★★☆☆

    Take one photo and get it from a phone to a laptop in three different ways (cloud, cable/USB, wireless share). Time each one and note which needed the internet.

    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    Cloud: upload to Drive, download on laptop. Wireless: AirDrop / Nearby Share. Cable: plug the phone in and copy from its DCIM folder.

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án

    Typical result: wireless share ~10 s (no internet), cable ~30 s (no internet), cloud 1–2 min (internet twice: up and down). For ONE file nearby, wireless wins; for sharing with many people far away, the cloud wins.

    • Distance and size decide the road.
    4

    The 10-second video

    ★★★☆

    In Canva make a 2-page video: page 1 a title, page 2 one safety tip with an icon. 5 seconds each. Add a transition. Download as MP4 and play it on a phone.

    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    Timeline at the bottom: click the page → duration. Between pages → Add transition.

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án

    Success = the .mp4 plays on the phone with both pages visible for 5 s each and a smooth change between them. If text is cut off, it was too close to the edge — keep a margin.

    • Small first, then the full 6-scene video.
    5

    The full project + peer review

    ★★★★

    Build the whole SMART video from your storyboard, download the MP4, and show it to one classmate and one adult. Ask each: “Which tip did you remember best? What was hard to read?” Improve one thing and export again as v2.

    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    Name files v1, v2 — never overwrite the first version.

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án

    A good v2 usually has: bigger text, slower scenes (10–12 s), and the voice starting a moment after the text appears. Keep both files: v1 shows how much you improved.

    • Evaluate against criteria, then improve — the same loop as in Unit 2.

    Competitions for creative digital products

    The Hội thi Tin học trẻ toàn quốc (tinhoctre.vn) has a Bảng D1 — Sản phẩm sáng tạo (tiểu học) category: pupils submit a creative digital product (an educational game, an animation, a multimedia story) with a short presentation. Judges look for a clear purpose, creativity, technical skill and a good presentation — the same “purpose → criteria → evaluate” habit from this course. A SMART safety video with a voice-over and a one-page explanation of why you made it is a realistic first entry.

    Practice challenge (judge-style): make a 60-second video for Year 2 pupils (age 7) about ONE rule only — “Tell a trusted adult”. Criteria: ☐ a 7-year-old understands it without reading ☐ has a character and a tiny story ☐ under 60 s ☐ exported .mp4 ☐ you can explain in one minute why each scene is there.

    Real tools: Google Forms + Google Sheets. The Lab has a mini spreadsheet and a mini survey with auto-check; this tab does the real unit project — a class survey turned into a chart and a conclusion — in the real Google tools.

    The tools: Google Forms and Google Sheets

    Both are free websites that run in any browser and save automatically to Google Drive. Google Forms (forms.google.com) builds the survey and collects answers; Google Sheets (sheets.google.com) is the spreadsheet where you calculate and chart. At school you use your school Google account; at home a parent’s account works. On a tablet, install the “Google Sheets” app (Forms works in the browser).

    Forms map: the top has Questions and Responses tabs. Each question has a type menu (Multiple choice, Checkboxes, Short answer, Linear scale). The Send button gives a link. The Responses tab shows automatic charts and a green Sheets icon that opens all answers as a spreadsheet.

    Sheets map: the formula bar under the toolbar shows what is really in a cell. Insert → Chart makes a chart from selected cells; the Chart editor on the right lets you pick Bar/Column/Pie/Line and add a title. Data → Sort range orders rows. File → Download exports .xlsx or .pdf.

    The Lab’s Sheet and Survey tools copy these steps exactly — practise there first, then do it for real.

    Step by step: a class survey from question to chart

    1. 1

      Decide the question: “Which pet is most popular in 4A?” Go to forms.google.com → Blank form. Title: “Our Pets”.

    2. 2

      Question 1: type “Which pet do you have?”, choose Multiple choice, options Dog / Cat / Fish / Bird / None / Other. Question 2 (number): “How many pets in total?” → Short answer. No name question!

    3. 3

      Click Send → link icon 🔗 → Copy. Share the link with the class (teacher’s chat). Wait for 20+ responses.

    4. 4

      Open the Responses tab: Google already draws a pie chart for question 1. Click the green Sheets icon → Create a new spreadsheet.

    5. 5

      In Sheets, make a summary table: A1 “Pet”, B1 “Count”; A2–A6 the pet names; in B2 type =COUNTIF(C:C,"Dog") (column C holds the answers) — or count by hand for now. B7: =SUM(B2:B6).

    6. 6

      Select A1:B6 → Insert → Chart → Chart type: Column chart. Add a title “Pets in 4A”. Then try Pie chart and decide which tells the story better.

    7. 7

      Write three sentences of analysis under the chart (most, least, one surprise), and one limit (“only 4A, 24 answers”). File → Download → PDF to present.

    Model project — “How do we get to school?” (24 answers)

    Question: How do pupils in 4A travel to school, and how long does it take? Form: Q1 “How do you usually get to school?” (Multiple choice: Walk / Bicycle / Car / Bus / Motorbike / Other). Q2 “About how many minutes does it take?” (Short answer, number). Expected outcome: a Sheet with a summary table, a column chart of Q1, the average of Q2, and 3 sentences of analysis.

    ABC
    1WayPupilsFormula used
    2Car9=COUNTIF(Answers!B:B,A2)
    copied down
    3Motorbike7
    4Bus4
    5Walk3
    6Bicycle1
    7Other0
    8Total24=SUM(B2:B7)
    9Avg minutes18.5=AVERAGE(Answers!C:C)
    • Analysis: “Car is the most common (9 of 24, more than a third). Only 4 pupils walk or cycle. The average trip is 18.5 minutes; the longest was 40 (bus).”
    • Limit: “24 pupils, one class, one week in the rainy season — walking might be higher in dry weather.”
    • New question: “Do pupils who live closer walk more? Next time ask the distance too.”

    Practice tasks on the real tools, easy to hard. Each has a model answer.

    1

    Ten cells

    ★☆☆☆

    In a new Google Sheet type the days Mon–Fri in A1:A5 and these temperatures in B1:B5: 31, 33, 29, 35, 32. In B6 write a formula for the average; in B7 the maximum.

    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    Start each formula with =. The range is B1:B5.

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án

    =AVERAGE(B1:B5) → 32 · =MAX(B1:B5) → 35. Check by hand: 31+33+29+35+32 = 160, 160 ÷ 5 = 32.

    • Click B6 and look at the formula bar: it shows the formula, the cell shows 32.
    2

    Chart it two ways

    ★★☆☆

    Using the pet table (Dog 8, Cat 6, Fish 4, Bird 2, None 5), insert a column chart and then a pie chart. Give both a title. Write one sentence: which chart answers “which pet is most popular?” faster?

    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    Select A1:B6 first, then Insert → Chart. Change the type in the Chart editor → Setup → Chart type.

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án

    The column chart answers it faster — the tallest bar jumps out. The pie shows that Dog is about one third of the class, which the bars do not say directly. Both are correct; they answer different questions.

    • “Compare” → bars. “Part of the whole” → pie.
    3

    Sort and find

    ★★☆☆

    Type 8 classmates’ first names (no surnames!) in A and their number of siblings in B. Sort the range by column B, largest first. Then use MIN, MAX and AVERAGE in B10:B12.

    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    Select A1:B8 → Data → Sort range → Advanced → Sort by column B → Z→A.

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án

    After sorting, row 1 holds the pupil with the most siblings. MIN is usually 0 (an only child), MAX 2–4, AVERAGE around 1–1.5. Notice the formulas still work after sorting because the range B1:B8 did not change.

    • Sort the whole range, never just one column — or names and numbers separate!
    4

    Build a form and read the responses

    ★★★☆

    Create a Google Form “Favourite fruit” with one multiple-choice question (Apple / Banana / Mango / Orange / Other) and one number question (“How many pieces of fruit per day?”). Send it to at least 10 family members or classmates. Open Responses and describe the automatic charts.

    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    Multiple choice → Google draws a pie chart. A number question → a bar chart of the values.

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án

    Responses shows: Q1 as a pie chart with percentages (parts of a whole — everyone picked one fruit); Q2 as a bar chart of how many people answered 1, 2, 3… The green Sheets icon opens the raw table: one row per person, one column per question, plus a timestamp column.

    • No “name” question — you do not need it and it is personal data.
    5

    The full project

    ★★★★

    Choose your own question about the class (sleep, screen time, sports, breakfast…). Build the form (2–3 closed questions, no personal data), collect 20+ answers, open in Sheets, make a summary table with COUNTIF or by hand, add SUM/AVERAGE/MAX, insert the right chart, and write 3 sentences of analysis + 1 limit + 1 new question. Export as PDF.

    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    Follow the model project structure exactly; swap in your topic.

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án

    A complete answer has: a neutral question with “Other”; 20+ rows in the answers sheet; a summary table whose total equals the number of responses (check with =SUM); a titled chart of the right type; analysis with numbers (“12 of 24 = half”); a limit; a new question. Marks are lost for a pie chart of numbers that are not parts of a whole, or a typed total instead of a formula.

    • Question → collect → organise → chart → conclude: all five boxes of the cycle.

    Data skills in competitions

    The Hội thi Tin học trẻ Bảng A (primary) is mostly programming, but many problems are secretly data problems: “read n numbers, print the largest / the total / the average” — exactly MAX, SUM and AVERAGE, done with loops in Scratch instead of a spreadsheet. Unit 5 shows those programs. The creative-product category (Bảng D1) also rewards projects that collect and present real data — a survey about your school with clear charts is a strong, honest entry.

    Practice challenge (judge-style): the school wants to reduce plastic. Design a 4-question survey about bottles and bags, collect 30 answers from two different year groups, and produce ONE page: one chart, three findings with numbers, one recommendation. Criteria: ☐ neutral questions ☐ two year groups compared ☐ chart type justified ☐ total in the table equals responses ☐ recommendation follows from the data, not from opinion.

    Real tools: Tinkercad (+ Canva for photos). The Lab trains the thinking (sorting benefits and risks, editing an image, planning robot parts); this tab builds the real unit project — a 3D robot model that solves a problem — in Tinkercad.

    The tool: Tinkercad (free)

    Tinkercad runs at tinkercad.com in Chrome, Edge or Safari on a laptop (a mouse helps a lot; it also works on an iPad). It is free. Pupils under 13 sign in with a class code from the teacher (Tinkercad Classrooms) or with a personal account a parent approves. Everything saves automatically to your dashboard.

    Screen map: the big grid is the workplane; the right panel is the shape library (Basic Shapes: box, cylinder, sphere, cone, wedge…); the top bar has Undo, Copy/Paste, Delete, Group, Ungroup, Align, Mirror; the small panel that appears when you click a shape lets you choose Solid or Hole and a colour. Navigate: right-drag to orbit, scroll to zoom, the view cube top-left to snap to top/front views.

    Keys to remember: L Align · Ctrl+D Duplicate · Ctrl+G Group · Ctrl+Z Undo · H Hole · S Solid · F Fit view · arrow keys nudge 1 mm. Export (top-right) → .STL for 3D printing; Share → screenshot for your design page.

    First plan the robot in the Lab (task 4: problem, parts, why). Then build it here.

    Step by step: your problem-solving robot in Tinkercad

    1. 1

      Sign in → Create → 3D Design. Click the random name top-left and rename it, e.g. “DustBuddy”.

    2. 2

      Body: drag a Cylinder onto the workplane. Drag the white corner handle until the ruler says 60 × 60; drag the top white handle to 20 mm tall (low = fits under chairs).

    3. 3

      Wheels: drag another Cylinder, size 15 × 15 × 5. Rotate it 90° (hover, drag the curved arrow, watch for 90). Place it at the side of the body. Ctrl+D and move the copy to the other side.

    4. 4

      Sensors: a small Box 8 × 4 × 4 on the front edge = bump sensor. Two tiny Cylinders 4 mm on top = distance sensor “eyes”. Colour them differently (click shape → colour) so they are visible.

    5. 5

      Tool slot (the Hole trick): Box 30 × 10 × 6 → click Hole → push it into the bottom front of the body. Select body + hole → Group. You now have a slot for the brush.

    6. 6

      Line up: select everything (Ctrl+A) → L → click the middle dot of the left–right axis so the robot is symmetrical. Then Group everything except the wheels.

    7. 7

      Test against the problem: is the body ≤ 20 mm tall (fits under chairs)? Is the bump sensor at the front? Take a screenshot (Share → Download) for your design page and write one sentence per part: “___ because ___”.

    Model project — “DustBuddy”, the under-the-table crumb robot

    Problem: crumbs and dust under the dining table after dinner. User: a busy family with a cat — must be quiet, low, safe. Expected outcome: a Tinkercad model with 7 parts, a screenshot from the front and from above, and a design page with a “because” sentence for every part.

    PartTinkercad shape & size (mm)Because…
    Round bodyCylinder 60 × 60 × 20round so it does not get stuck in corners; low to fit under chairs
    2 wheelsCylinder 15 × 15 × 5, rotated 90°, ×2flat floor → wheels are enough, cheap and quiet
    Bump sensorBox 8 × 4 × 4 at the frontfeels chair legs and walls
    Distance sensor2 × Cylinder 4 × 4 × 3 on topslows down before hitting the cat
    Brush slotBox 30 × 10 × 6 as a Holebrush sweeps crumbs into the nozzle
    Vacuum nozzleBox 20 × 6 × 4 underneathsucks crumbs into the bin
    Battery bayBox 20 × 10 × 8 as a Hole at the backrechargeable at a dock; no cable for the cat to chew
    • Program idea (Unit 2 + 5): forever → if bump then turn 90°; if distance < 10 cm then speed = slow; if battery < 20% then go to dock.
    • Test question answered: “Under our chairs there is 22 cm — the 20 mm model scaled ×10 is 200 mm = 20 cm. Fits.”
    • Responsible-designer check: no camera (privacy), rounded edges (safety), stops when lifted (safety), recyclable battery.

    Practice tasks on the real tools, easy to hard. Each has a model answer.

    1

    Three shapes, one snowman

    ★☆☆☆

    In Tinkercad, stack three spheres of 30, 22 and 15 mm on top of each other, perfectly centred, and make the top one orange.

    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    Lift a shape with the black cone handle. Select all → L → click the centre dots.

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án

    Sphere 1 on the workplane; sphere 2 lifted to 30 mm (type 30 in the height box that appears when you drag the cone); sphere 3 lifted to 52 mm. Select all three → L → click the two middle dots (left–right and front–back). Click the top sphere → colour → orange. Group to make one object.

    • Align is more accurate than your eyes — use it every time.
    2

    The wheel with an axle hole

    ★★☆☆

    Make a wheel: cylinder 20 × 20 × 6, with a 4 mm round hole through the centre. Then duplicate it to get four identical wheels in a row.

    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    Small cylinder → Hole → centre it with Align → Group. Then Ctrl+D three times (each copy appears on top — drag it aside).

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án

    Cylinder 20×20×6 (solid). Cylinder 4×4×8 (taller than the wheel so it cuts right through) → Hole. Select both → L → centre dots → Group: a wheel with a hole. Ctrl+D, drag right 25 mm; repeat twice. Tip: after the first Ctrl+D and move, pressing Ctrl+D again repeats the same move automatically.

    • The hole must be TALLER than the solid or it leaves a thin skin.
    3

    Fix this photo

    ★★☆☆

    Take a photo of any object on a messy table with a phone. In Canva (or Photos): crop to the object, raise brightness, add a little contrast, then resize to 800 pixels wide and download as JPG. Compare the file sizes before and after.

    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    Canva: upload → click photo → Edit photo → Crop / Adjust. Resize: Share → Download → Size ✎.

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án

    Typical result: original 3–5 MB at 4000 px wide → edited 150–300 KB at 800 px. Order matters: crop and adjust first on the sharp original, resize last. The crop should leave a little space around the object, not cut it.

    • Same picture, 15× smaller file — that is why websites resize.
    4

    A robot for a new problem

    ★★★☆

    Problem: the school pond gets covered in fallen leaves. Plan a robot (problem, user, 5 parts with “because”), then build it in Tinkercad with at least one Hole and one Align. Screenshot front and top.

    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    It must float or fly. What senses leaves? What collects them?

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án

    One good design “LeafBoat”: flat wide body (box 80×40×15, floats); two paddle wheels (cylinders rotated, because water not ground); camera on a mast (sees leaf patches); a front net = wedge as a Hole cut into the bow (collects leaves); solar panel on top (pond is outdoors, sunny). User: the school gardener — a big ON button, returns to the edge when the net is full.

    • Different problem → different movement part. Wheels on water make no sense.

    The full project + design page

    ★★★★

    Choose a real problem at home or school. Complete all five design steps, build the robot in Tinkercad, edit two screenshots (crop, brighten, resize), and make a one-page Canva design sheet: problem, user, labelled robot picture, a “because” for every part, and one risk with how you reduce it.

    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    Use the DustBuddy table as your template.

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án

    A complete page has: a one-sentence problem with who/where; the user’s needs; a picture where every part has a label line; 5–7 “because” sentences that each mention the problem or user; one risk (e.g. “could frighten the cat”) and its fix (“slows down within 10 cm”). Marks are lost for parts with no reason, and for screenshots that are dark or uncropped.

    • The design page is the artifact — the robot model is the evidence.

    Competitions for young designers

    Vietnam’s Robotacon and VEX IQ school leagues start from primary age with real robots that sense, think and act — teams build a robot for a set challenge and explain their design to judges. The Hội thi Tin học trẻ Bảng D1 (creative products, primary) accepts design projects too: a Tinkercad robot model with a clear problem, a design page and a short video counts as a creative digital product. Judges everywhere score the same three things you practised here: a clear problem, a reason for every part, evidence of testing.

    Practice challenge (judge-style): “Design a robot that helps an elderly neighbour who lives alone.” 30 minutes to plan, 45 to build in Tinkercad, 3 minutes to present. Criteria: ☐ you interviewed (or imagined in detail) the user ☐ at least 2 sensors, each with a reason ☐ one safety feature ☐ one privacy decision ☐ a change you made after testing.

    Real Scratch. The Lab drills variables and operators with auto-check; this tab builds the unit project — the Air Quality Program — in MIT’s Scratch 3, then goes further with graded exercises and seven real contest problems.

    Real Scratch, two new palettes

    Open scratch.mit.edu/projects/editor (see Unit 2 → Scratch → Setup for accounts, saving and Vietnamese menus). This unit lives in two palettes: Variables (orange) — click Make a Variable, type a name like aqi, keep “For all sprites”, OK; you get set, change by, show/hide variable and the round reporter — and Operators (green) — the maths blocks in the table in Theory 2.

    Dropping reporters: round blocks fit into white oval slots. Drag the orange aqi reporter into the left slot of <; type 51 in the right slot; drag the whole < into the hexagon slot of if. To nest maths, build the inner block first, then drop it into the outer one. If a drop does not “click”, the slot highlights white when you are close enough.

    Watching values: tick the checkbox next to a variable in the palette to show its monitor on the stage. Right-click the monitor for a slider — great for testing the AQI program without typing: slide to 50, 51, 100, 101…

    Do Lab tasks 1–3 first (auto-checked). Then build the same ideas here, in real Scratch, with real saving.

    Step by step: the Air Quality Program

    1. 1

      New project. Variables → Make a Variable → name it aqi. Tick its checkbox so the monitor shows on stage.

    2. 2

      Events → when 🏁 clicked. Sensing → ask “Enter the AQI number:” and wait. Variables → set aqi to … and drop the Sensing answer reporter into its slot.

      when 🏁 clicked
      ask Enter the AQI number: and wait
      set aqi ▾ to answer
    3. 3

      Control → if / else. Operators → <: put aqi left, 51 right; drop into the if. In the “if” mouth: Looks → say (join aqi “ – Good 🟢 Play outside!”) for 3 seconds. Test: 🏁, type 42 → Good.

      if aqi < 51 then
      say join aqi – Good 🟢 Play outside! for 3 seconds
      else
    4. 4

      In the “else” mouth, drop ANOTHER if/else: aqi < 101 → Moderate 🟡. Keep nesting: < 151 → Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups 🟠, < 201 → Unhealthy 🔴, < 301 → Very Unhealthy 🟣, and the final else → Hazardous 🟤. Tip: right-click a finished if/else → Duplicate, then edit the number and text.

    5. 5

      Guard against bad input: wrap everything in one more if/else at the top — if (aqi < 0) or (aqi > 500) then say “Invalid: AQI must be 0–500”, else → the level chain.

      if aqi < 0 or aqi > 500 then
      say Invalid: AQI must be 0–500 for 2 seconds
      else
      …
    6. 6

      Run the test table from Theory 6: 42, 50, 51, 100, 101, 300, 301, −5, 600. Every result must match. Then File → Save to your computer as AirQuality.sb3.

    7. 7

      Make it yours: change the backdrop colour for each level (Looks → switch backdrop to), or add a sprite that puts on a mask when AQI > 100.

    Model project 1 — Air Quality Program (the unit project)

    Purpose: turn an AQI number into a level and advice, using the official six ranges, and refuse impossible numbers. Expected outcome: exactly the test table in Theory 6.

    when 🏁 clicked
    ask Enter the AQI number: and wait
    set aqi ▾ to answer
    if aqi < 0 or aqi > 500 then
    say Invalid: AQI must be 0–500 for 2 seconds
    else
    if aqi < 51 then
    say join aqi – Good 🟢 Play outside! for 3 seconds
    else
    if aqi < 101 then
    say join aqi – Moderate 🟡 Fine for most people for 3 seconds
    else
    if aqi < 151 then
    say join aqi – Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups 🟠 Wear a mask for 3 seconds
    else
    if aqi < 201 then
    say join aqi – Unhealthy 🔴 Limit time outside for 3 seconds
    else
    if aqi < 301 then
    say join aqi – Very Unhealthy 🟣 Stay indoors for 3 seconds
    else
    say join aqi – Hazardous 🟤 Emergency! for 3 seconds
    • The invalid check comes FIRST, so a negative number never reaches the level chain.
    • Each level uses < (next boundary + 1): 51, 101, 151, 201, 301 — the edge values from the official table.
    • join puts the number back into the sentence so the user sees what they typed.

    Model project 2 — Average of any amount of numbers

    Purpose: keep asking for numbers until the user types 0, then say the average. Expected outcome: 5, 7, 9, 0 → “Average: 7”.

    when 🏁 clicked
    set total ▾ to 0
    set count ▾ to 0
    ask Number? (0 to finish) and wait
    repeat until answer = 0
    change total ▾ by answer
    change count ▾ by 1
    ask Number? (0 to finish) and wait
    if count = 0 then
    say No numbers!
    else
    say join Average: total ÷ count
    • repeat until answer = 0 — the loop ends the moment 0 is typed, and 0 is NOT added.
    • count = 0 check avoids dividing by zero when the user types 0 straight away.

    Model project 3 — Times table with a counter

    Purpose: ask for a number n and print n × 1 … n × 10, one line per second. Expected outcome: n = 7 → “1 × 7 = 7”, “2 × 7 = 14”, … “10 × 7 = 70”.

    when 🏁 clicked
    ask Which table? and wait
    set n ▾ to answer
    set i ▾ to 0
    repeat 10
    change i ▾ by 1
    say join i join × join n join = i × n for 1 seconds
    • Four joins build one line: i, “ × ”, n, “ = ”, i × n.
    • say … for 1 seconds gives the reader time; without the seconds only the last line would be visible.

    Eight exercises, easy to hard. Build each in real Scratch, test with the table, then compare with the solution.

    Minutes to hours

    ★★☆☆

    Ask for a number of minutes and say it as hours and minutes, e.g. 135 → “2 h 15 min”.

    InputOutput

    5

    Largest of three

    ★★★☆

    Ask for three numbers and say the largest.

    InputOutput
    3 9 5Largest: 9
    7 7 2Largest: 7
    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    Set max to a; if b > max then set max to b; same for c.

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án
    when 🏁 clicked
    ask a? and wait
    set a ▾ to answer
    ask b? and wait
    set b ▾ to answer
    ask c? and wait
    set c ▾ to answer
    set max ▾ to a
    if b > max then
    set max ▾ to b
    if c > max then
    set max ▾ to c
    say join Largest: max
    • This “keep the best so far” pattern works for any number of inputs — it is how MAX works inside a spreadsheet.

    Sum 1 to n

    Ask for n and say 1 + 2 + … + n.

    InputOutput

    AQI with a week of readings
