    Numbers are the heart of Bảng A

    Look at the seven real problems below (district and provincial rounds, 2024–2025): every one is ask → variables → arithmetic → say, plus a loop with a counter. The Unit 2 competition page explained the contest itself; this page trains the number patterns that appear in almost every paper: round up a division (mod trick), last digit (mod 10), running sum with a counter, keep the best so far, slide two variables, and convert to one unit.

    How to work a problem: (1) copy the sample input/output into a test table; (2) write the formula in words; (3) build ask/set blocks for every input in the given order; (4) build the maths inside-out; (5) run every sample; (6) check the limits — if n can be 109, a loop to n will time out, look for a formula. More papers: scratch.hourofcode.vn — Thư viện đề thi.

    1

    Sa bàn (Arenas) — Liên Chiểu, Đà Nẵng 2025, Câu 2

    Tin học trẻ Bảng A, quận Liên Chiểu, Đà Nẵng 2025 ↗

    M schools take part, each with N teams. Each arena holds at most K teams. What is the smallest number of arenas needed? Input: M, N, K (1 ≤ M, N, K ≤ 109). Output: the number of arenas.

    InputOutput
    10 2 45
    ▸How to think about it · Cách suy nghĩHide the approach · Ẩn cách suy nghĩ

    Total teams = M × N. Divide by K and round UP: if it divides exactly that is the answer, otherwise one more arena for the leftovers (Unit 2’s grouping problem again, with a multiplication first).

    ▸Full Scratch solution · Lời giải Scratch đầy đủFull Scratch solution · Lời giải Scratch đầy đủ
    when 🏁 clicked
    ask M and wait
    set M ▾ to answer
    ask N and wait
    set N ▾ to answer
    ask K and wait
    set K ▾ to answer
    set total ▾ to M × N
    set s ▾ to floor ▾ of total ÷ K
    if total mod K > 0 then
    change s ▾ by 1
    say s
    • 10 × 2 = 20 teams; 20 ÷ 4 = 5 exactly → 5. With K = 3: 20 ÷ 3 = 6 rem 2 → 7.
    • Never loop up to M × N — it can be 1018. Formulas with mod are instant.
    2

    Dãy số (Sequence) — Tiên Du, Bắc Ninh 2025, Bài 3

    Tin học trẻ Bảng A, huyện Tiên Du, Bắc Ninh 2025 ↗

    The sequence 1, 3, 7, 13, 21, … Find the n-th number. Input: n (1 ≤ n ≤ 107). Output: the n-th term.

    InputOutput
    521
    11
    ▸How to think about it · Cách suy nghĩHide the approach · Ẩn cách suy nghĩ

    Differences are 2, 4, 6, 8 — they grow by 2. Either loop n − 1 times adding 2, 4, 6, … or spot the formula: term = n × n − n + 1 (check: 5 × 5 − 5 + 1 = 21).

    ▸Full Scratch solution · Lời giải Scratch đầy đủFull Scratch solution · Lời giải Scratch đầy đủ
    when 🏁 clicked
    ask n and wait
    set n ▾ to answer
    say n × n − n + 1
    • Loop version: set t to 1, set d to 2, repeat n − 1 { change t by d; change d by 2 } — same answer, slower for n = 107.
    • Build the formula inside-out: n × n, then − n, then + 1.
    3

    Tổng dãy số (Sum of a sequence) — Liên Chiểu, Đà Nẵng 2025, Câu 4

    Tin học trẻ Bảng A, quận Liên Chiểu, Đà Nẵng 2025 ↗

    The sequence 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, … (every number that is not a multiple of 3). Compute the sum of the first N numbers. Input: N. Output: the sum.

    InputOutput
    412
    737
    ▸How to think about it · Cách suy nghĩHide the approach · Ẩn cách suy nghĩ

    Walk through the whole numbers 1, 2, 3, …; skip any with i mod 3 = 0; add the others and count them until you have N. Two counters: i (the number) and count (how many taken).

    ▸Full Scratch solution · Lời giải Scratch đầy đủFull Scratch solution · Lời giải Scratch đầy đủ
    when 🏁 clicked
    ask N and wait
    set N ▾ to answer
    set i ▾ to 0
    set count ▾ to 0
    set sum ▾ to 0
    repeat until count = N
    change i ▾ by 1
    if not i mod 3 = 0 then
    change sum ▾ by i
    change count ▾ by 1
    say sum
    • N = 4: takes 1, 2, 4, 5 → 12 ✓. N = 7: 1+2+4+5+7+8+10 = 37.
    • repeat until count = N stops exactly when enough numbers are collected.
    4

    Số gần tròn chục (Near-tens) — Tiên Du, Bắc Ninh 2025, Bài 4

    Tin học trẻ Bảng A, huyện Tiên Du, Bắc Ninh 2025 ↗

    A “near-ten” number ends in 9 or 1. Given n, count the near-ten numbers smaller than n. Input: n (1 ≤ n ≤ 1012). Output: the count.

    InputOutput
    163
    102
    ▸How to think about it · Cách suy nghĩHide the approach · Ẩn cách suy nghĩ

    The last digit of i is i mod 10. Loop i from 1 to n − 1; if i mod 10 = 1 or i mod 10 = 9, count it. (For the huge limit a formula is needed, but the loop earns most marks and teaches the idea.)

    ▸Full Scratch solution · Lời giải Scratch đầy đủFull Scratch solution · Lời giải Scratch đầy đủ
    when 🏁 clicked
    ask n and wait
    set n ▾ to answer
    set i ▾ to 0
    set count ▾ to 0
    repeat n − 1
    change i ▾ by 1
    if i mod 10 = 1 or i mod 10 = 9 then
    change count ▾ by 1
    say count
    • n = 16: 1, 9, 11 → 3 ✓. n = 10: 1, 9 → 2.
    • “mod 10” = last digit is a trick worth memorising; “mod 100” gives the last two digits.
    5

    Tổng các số chẵn (Sum of the evens) — Hậu Giang 2025, Bài 2

    Tin học trẻ Bảng A, tỉnh Hậu Giang 2025 ↗

    Five different natural numbers A, B, C, D, E (0 < each < 100). Print the sum of the even ones. If any number breaks the rule, print “Khong thoa man de bai”.

    InputOutput
    1 2 3 4 56
    100 2 3 4 5Khong thoa man de bai
    ▸How to think about it · Cách suy nghĩHide the approach · Ẩn cách suy nghĩ

    Read the five numbers in a loop; while reading, check the range and add evens to a total. Use a flag variable ok (1 = fine). At the end, if ok = 1 say the total, else the message.

    ▸Full Scratch solution · Lời giải Scratch đầy đủFull Scratch solution · Lời giải Scratch đầy đủ
    when 🏁 clicked
    set total ▾ to 0
    set ok ▾ to 1
    repeat 5
    ask Number? and wait
    if answer < 1 or answer > 99 then
    set ok ▾ to 0
    if answer mod 2 = 0 then
    change total ▾ by answer
    if ok = 1 then
    say total
    else
    say Khong thoa man de bai
    • The rule “0 < x < 100” becomes “x < 1 or x > 99 → not ok” for whole numbers.
    • A flag variable remembers that something went wrong, even if later numbers are fine.
    6

    Tìm số thứ N của dãy (Fibonacci-style) — Nha Trang 2024, Câu 2

    Tin học trẻ Bảng A, TP Nha Trang 2024 ↗

    Input the first number, the second number, and N. Each later number is the sum of the two before it. Print the N-th number (only the answer, not the whole sequence).

    InputOutput
    1 1 713
    2 3 48
    ▸How to think about it · Cách suy nghĩHide the approach · Ẩn cách suy nghĩ

    Keep two variables a and b (the last two numbers). N − 2 times: c = a + b, then slide: a = b, b = c. The answer is b. The ORDER of the three set blocks matters.

    ▸Full Scratch solution · Lời giải Scratch đầy đủFull Scratch solution · Lời giải Scratch đầy đủ
    when 🏁 clicked
    ask First number and wait
    set a ▾ to answer
    ask Second number and wait
    set b ▾ to answer
    ask N and wait
    set N ▾ to answer
    repeat N − 2
    set c ▾ to a + b
    set a ▾ to b
    set b ▾ to c
    say b
    • 1 1 7: after 5 turns b goes 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 ✓. 2 3 4: 5, 8 ✓.
    • If N is 1 or 2 the loop runs 0 (or −1 → 0) times and b is wrong for N = 1 — add “if N = 1 then say a” for full marks.
    7

    Thời gian (Arrival time) — Long An 2025, Bài 3

    Tin học trẻ Bảng A, tỉnh Long An 2025 ↗

    The cat walks 120 steps from A to B. Input the speed v (steps per hour), the start hour (0–23) and start minute (0–59). Round the minutes. If the time passes 23:59, wrap to a 24-hour clock. Output: “Bạn sẽ đến B lúc [giờ] giờ [phút] phút”.

    InputOutput
    50 5 5Bạn sẽ đến B lúc 7 giờ 29 phút
    70 23 50Bạn sẽ đến B lúc 1 giờ 33 phút
    ▸How to think about it · Cách suy nghĩHide the approach · Ẩn cách suy nghĩ

    Work entirely in minutes. Travel = round(120 ÷ v × 60). Start = h × 60 + m. Arrival = start + travel. Hour = floor(arrival ÷ 60) mod 24 (the mod wraps past midnight); minute = arrival mod 60.

    ▸Full Scratch solution · Lời giải Scratch đầy đủFull Scratch solution · Lời giải Scratch đầy đủ
    when 🏁 clicked
    ask v and wait
    set v ▾ to answer
    ask hour and wait
    set h ▾ to answer
    ask minute and wait
    set m ▾ to answer
    set travel ▾ to round ▾ of 120 ÷ v × 60
    set arr ▾ to h × 60 + m + travel
    say join Bạn sẽ đến B lúc join floor ▾ of arr ÷ 60 mod 24 join giờ join arr mod 60 phút
    • 50 5 5: travel 120 ÷ 50 = 2.4 h = 144 min; start 305; arrival 449 → 7 h 29 ✓.
    • 70 23 50: travel 102.86 → 103; start 1430; arrival 1533 → floor 25 mod 24 = 1, 1533 mod 60 = 33 ✓.
    • Converting everything to one unit (minutes) is the key move in every time problem.

    Real tools: Canva + Tinkercad. The Lab’s network builder checks whether your packets can really travel; this tab produces the unit project — the Dolphin Tracking Center diagram, 3D station and explanation — with the real tools.

    The tools: Canva for the network diagram, Tinkercad for the 3D centre

    The unit project has two parts. The network diagram — which devices, which links — is drawn in Canva (Unit 1 → Setup): use Elements → Lines for cables (solid) and wireless (dashed), Elements → search “router”, “laptop”, “satellite”, “dolphin” for icons, and text boxes for labels. Canva also has a Whiteboard type that is perfect for diagrams.

    The 3D model of the Dolphin Tracking Center — the building, the satellite dish, the antenna mast, the server room — is built in Tinkercad (Unit 4 → Setup for sign-in, shapes, Hole and Group). Nothing new to install: you already know both tools.

    Diagram rules: one icon per device; every link is a line; solid = cable, dashed = wireless, a curved dashed line to the sky = satellite; every device gets a label; the router sits between the inside and the outside; add a legend box that explains the line styles.

    Build the network first in the Lab (task 3 — the checker tells you if a packet can get from the dolphin to the server). Then draw and model it here.

    Step by step: the Dolphin Tracking Center

    1. 1

      List the devices (from Theory 5): dolphin tag (sensor), satellite, ground-station dish + router, the centre’s router, switch, server, access point, 3 researcher tablets, and the internet cloud between the two routers.

    2. 2

      Canva → Create a design → Whiteboard. Place icons left to right in the order data travels: sea → sky → ground station → cloud → centre. Elements → search each icon; drag; resize to the same height.

    3. 3

      Draw the links. Elements → Lines: a dashed curved line tag → satellite → dish; a solid thick line dish-router → cloud → centre router (fibre); solid lines router → switch → server; dashed lines access point → tablets. Colour cables blue and wireless orange.

    4. 4

      Label everything with a text box: device name + its job in 3 words (“Router — chooses route”). Add a legend: “— cable · - - wireless · ~ satellite”.

    5. 5

      Add the backup link (Example 3): a second dashed line from the centre router to a 4G tower or a satellite dish, labelled “backup — if fibre breaks”. This is the mark of a designer who tested.

    6. 6

      Tinkercad: a flat Box 120 × 80 × 30 (the building); a Cylinder 10 × 10 × 60 on the roof (mast) with a small Sphere on top (antenna); a Paraboloid or a half Sphere tilted 45° (satellite dish); a Box 30 × 20 × 20 as a Hole in the side wall → Group (the server-room door). Align (L) the mast to the roof centre.

    7. 7

      Export: Canva → Share → Download → PNG; Tinkercad → Share → screenshot. Put both on one Canva page with a 4-sentence explanation: what the centre does, how data travels, which link is weakest, how you protected it.

    Model project — Dolphin Tracking Center (design sheet)

    Purpose: receive positions from 12 tagged dolphins every time they surface and show them on a live map for 6 researchers. Expected outcome: a labelled network diagram with 11 devices and 3 link types, a backup link, a 3D model of the station, and a written explanation.

    DeviceTypeLink inLink outBecause…
    Dolphin tag ×12Sensor—Satelliteopen sea: no towers, no cables
    SatelliteRelaySatelliteSatellitesees both the sea and the station
    Ground-station dish + routerRouterSatelliteFibrethe door from sky to internet
    InternetWANFibreFibrestation is 300 km from the centre
    Centre routerRouterFibre (+ 4G backup)Cablethe centre’s door; two roads in
    SwitchSwitchCableCablejoins server + access point
    ServerServerCable—stores every position; draws the map
    Access pointAPCableWi-Firesearchers walk around
    Tablets ×6ClientWi-Fi—view the map anywhere in the building
    • Data path (5 hops): tag → satellite → dish → fibre/internet → centre router → switch → server → access point → tablet.
    • Weakest link: the single fibre. Fix: 4G backup router; ground station stores readings while the link is down.
    • Safety: Wi-Fi password; server only reachable from inside the LAN; https for the public map.

    Practice tasks on the real tools, easy to hard. Each has a model answer.

    1

    Map your home

    ★☆☆☆

    In Canva, draw your real home network: the ISP box, every device you can find, solid lines for cables and dashed for Wi-Fi. Label each device.

    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    Look at the back of the ISP box: each lit cable port = one wired device.

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án

    A typical answer: ISP box (router+switch+AP) with a fibre line to the wall; TV and maybe a PC on cables; 3–6 phones/tablets/laptops on Wi-Fi; a smart speaker on Wi-Fi. The box is in the middle; the internet cloud is outside.

    • Most homes have more wireless than wired devices — and one router.
    2

    Wired or wireless?

    ★★☆☆

    For each device decide the best link and write why: a desktop PC in the study, a robot vacuum, a printer next to the router, a phone in the garden, a weather sensor on the roof, a fishing boat 50 km out.

    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    Does it move? How far? Is there a plug?

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án

    PC → cable (never moves, wants speed). Robot vacuum → Wi-Fi (moves around the house). Printer → cable (next to router, never moves). Phone in garden → Wi-Fi if in range, else 4G. Roof sensor → Wi-Fi (or a long-range low-power radio; no cable up there). Fishing boat → satellite (no towers at sea) or 4G near the coast.

    • Reach, movement and reliability decide.
    3

    Follow a packet

    ★★☆☆

    Write the journey of ONE packet from a tablet in the Dolphin Tracking Center asking the server for the map — and the reply packet coming back. Name every device it passes.

    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    Both are inside the centre’s LAN — the packet never needs the router.

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án

    Request: tablet → (Wi-Fi) → access point → (cable) → switch → (cable) → server. Reply: server → switch → access point → tablet. The router and the internet are not used because the server is inside the same LAN — that is why the map still works when the fibre is cut.

    • Inside the LAN, the switch does all the work.
    4

    Break it, fix it

    ★★★☆

    On your Dolphin diagram, cross out one link at a time (satellite, fibre, switch cable, Wi-Fi) and write what stops working. Then add the cheapest fix for the worst break.

    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    Which break loses DATA (not just the view)?

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án

    Satellite down → no new positions at all (worst, but you cannot fix a satellite — tags store readings and resend). Fibre cut → centre blind; fix: 4G backup router (cheap). Switch cable to server cut → nobody sees the map; fix: spare cable, 2 minutes. Wi-Fi down → tablets blind but the server still records; fix: a second access point. Cheapest important fix: the 4G backup.

    • Store-and-forward at the ground station means a broken link delays data instead of losing it.
    5

    The full project

    ★★★★

    Produce the complete Dolphin Tracking Center: Canva diagram (all devices, 3 link types, legend, backup link), Tinkercad model of the station (building, mast, dish, one Hole), and a one-page explanation covering purpose, data path, weakest link and safety. Present it in 2 minutes.

    ▸Show hint · Xem gợi ýHide hint · Ẩn gợi ý

    Use the model design sheet as your checklist.

    ▸Show solution · Xem đáp ánHide solution · Ẩn đáp án

    A complete answer: every device from the model table appears with the right link style; the packet path can be traced with a finger from fin to tablet without a gap; the backup link is labelled; the 3D station has a dish pointing up and a visible door; the explanation says WHY satellite at sea and cable indoors. Marks are lost for a switch connected to the internet directly, for missing labels, or for a diagram with no wireless lines.

    • Diagram + model + explanation = the unit’s three artifacts.

    Networks in competitions

    Network design appears in the Hội thi Tin học trẻ Bảng D (creative products) as “smart” projects — a smart school, a smart farm, a flood-warning system — where judges ask exactly the questions in this unit: which sensors, which links, what if one fails, how is it kept safe? Internationally, the Bebras computational-thinking challenge (Vietnam takes part every November) has network puzzles for primary pupils: shortest routes, which link to cut, how packets get reordered. The Lab’s network tool is good practice for both.

    Practice challenge (judge-style): design the network for a flood-warning system on a river near a village: water-level sensors on 3 bridges, a siren in the village, a screen at the school, and a laptop at the district office 40 km away. Criteria: ☐ every sensor has a link that works in a storm ☐ the siren still works if the internet is down ☐ the district office sees the data ☐ one backup link ☐ one safety rule (who can trigger the siren?).

    Vocabulary table

    The important English words from this unit, with their Vietnamese meaning and an example sentence taken from the lesson itself.

    Algorithm
    Thuật toán

    An algorithm is a set of clear, step-by-step instructions to do a task.

    Algorithm (Thuật toán) là một tập hợp các chỉ dẫn rõ ràng, từng bước, để làm một việc.

    Selection
    Lựa chọn (rẽ nhánh)

    Selection means the computer chooses what to do next based on a question.

    Selection (Lựa chọn) nghĩa là máy tính chọn việc làm tiếp theo dựa trên một câu hỏi.

    Condition
    Điều kiện

    Selection always starts with a condition — a question whose answer is true or false.

    Selection luôn bắt đầu bằng một Condition (Điều kiện) — câu hỏi có câu trả lời là true hoặc false.

    Binary
    Nhị phân (gồm hai)

    The word binary means “made of two”.

    Từ Binary (Nhị phân) nghĩa là “gồm hai”.

    Boolean
    Giá trị đúng/sai

    A true/false value is called a Boolean.

    Giá trị true/false được gọi là Boolean.

    Comparison operator
    Phép so sánh

    The Operators group gives us three comparison operators: =, > and <.

    Nhóm Operators cho ta ba Comparison operators (Phép so sánh): =, > và <.

    Event
    Sự kiện

    Every Scratch program starts with an event — a hat block such as when 🏁 clicked.

    Mọi chương trình Scratch đều bắt đầu bằng một Event (Sự kiện) — khối mũ như when 🏁 clicked.

    Input
    Đầu vào

    It often takes an input with the ask … and wait block.

    Nó thường nhận một Input (Đầu vào) bằng khối ask … and wait.

    Output
    Đầu ra

    The decision block checks the answer and produces an output, usually with say.

    Khối quyết định kiểm tra câu trả lời và tạo ra Output (Đầu ra), thường bằng khối say.

    Variable
    Biến số

    A variable is a named box that remembers a number — perfect for keeping score.

    Variable (Biến số) là một chiếc hộp có tên để nhớ một con số — rất hợp để giữ điểm.

    Bug
    Lỗi chương trình

    Tracing is the fastest way to find a bug (a mistake in the code).

    Lần theo là cách nhanh nhất để tìm Bug (Lỗi) trong mã.

    Evaluate
    Đánh giá

    Finally, evaluate the program against its criteria — a checklist written from the purpose.

    Cuối cùng, hãy Evaluate (Đánh giá) chương trình theo tiêu chí — một danh sách kiểm tra viết ra từ mục đích.

    Level 1 — Multiple choice

    Did you know?

    • In 1847 the English mathematician George Boole wrote down the maths of true and false. Every IF block in Scratch still uses his “Boolean” logic — more than 175 years later.Source: Britannica — George Boole ↗
    • The first real computer “bug” was a moth! In 1947 engineers found one stuck inside the Harvard Mark II computer and taped it into their logbook — that is why we still say “bug” and “debug”.Source: Smithsonian National Museum of American History ↗
    • The word bit is short for “binary digit” — a single 0 or 1. It was invented in January 1947 by John Tukey, and everything on your computer is made of billions of them.Source: Wikipedia — Bit ↗
    • ENIAC, finished in 1946, was one of the first electronic computers. It had almost 18 000 glass vacuum tubes and about one of them burned out every day or two!Source: Computer History Museum ↗
    • Scratch was first released in 2007. By December 2024 more than 164 million projects had been shared on the Scratch website — many of them quizzes just like yours.Source: Scratch Wiki ↗

    Binary decisions in real life

    Traffic lights

    IF the light is red THEN cars stop, ELSE they may go — a binary decision every driver follows.

    Air conditioner

    IF room temperature > 25°C THEN start cooling. The condition uses a comparison operator, just like Scratch.

    Lift doors

    IF something is blocking the door THEN open again, ELSE close. Selection keeps people safe.

    Phone unlock

    IF the passcode = the saved code THEN unlock, ELSE say “Try again”. Exactly your quiz, in disguise!

    Washing machine

    IF the door is closed THEN start, ELSE show a warning light.

    Video games

    IF the player touches a coin THEN change score by 1. Games are full of IF blocks running many times a second.

    Glossary

    Algorithm
    A set of clear, step-by-step instructions to do a task.
    Selection
    The part of an algorithm where the computer chooses between paths based on a condition.
    Condition
    A question that is either true or false, such as “answer = yes”.
    Boolean
    A value that can only be true or false. The pointed blocks in Scratch report Booleans.
    Comparison operator
    A block that compares two values: = (equal), > (greater than), < (less than).
    Event
    Something that starts a script, like clicking the green flag or pressing a key.
    Input
    Information that goes INTO a program — for example what the player types after “ask”.
    Output
    What the program shows or does as a result — for example the sprite saying “Correct!”.
    Variable
    A named box that stores a value that can change, like score.
    Bug / Debug
    A bug is a mistake in a program; debugging is finding and fixing it.
    Trace
    Reading a program step by step to predict what it will do for a given input.
    Criteria
    The checklist a program must meet to be “finished” — written from its purpose.

    Try it yourself: go on a binary-decision hunt around your home today! The washing machine, the lift, traffic lights, an app on a parent’s phone. For each one write: IF … THEN … ELSE … How many can you find in one day?

    Did you know?

    • The first email over a network was sent in 1971 by Ray Tomlinson — and he is the reason every address has an @ sign.Source: Internet Hall of Fame ↗
    • The QWERTY keyboard layout is over 150 years old: Christopher Sholes sold his typewriter design to Remington in 1873, and by 1891 more than 100 000 QWERTY typewriters were in use.Source: Smithsonian Magazine ↗
    • More than 500 hours of video are uploaded to YouTube every single minute — published instantly, to the whole world.Source: Statista ↗
    • The first USB flash drives went on sale in 2000 and held just 8 MB — about two photos today. A modern stick holds thousands of times more.Source: StorageNewsletter ↗
    • In 2024 about 5.5 billion people — 68% of everyone on Earth — were online. Whatever you publish can, in theory, reach all of them.Source: ITU Facts and Figures 2024 ↗

    Digital artifacts in real life

    A birthday video

    Photos + music + your voice = an advanced artifact, exported as .mp4 so Grandma can play it on her phone.

    Homework on a USB stick

    Save as .pdf, copy to the stick, plug into the school computer — no internet needed.

    Class photos in Google Drive

    The teacher uploads once; every family opens the link on any device.

    USB-C vs USB-A

    A new stick will not fit an old laptop port — hardware compatibility needs an adapter.

    A game high-score board

    Your nickname and score are published to every player instantly — choose a nickname without your real name.

    Chatting with a friend

    Touch-typing lets you answer quickly AND check what you wrote before you send it.

    Glossary

    Digital artifact
    Anything made on a computer and saved as a file — a poster, slideshow, recording or video.
    Media
    The four building blocks of artifacts: text, image, audio, video.
    File extension
    The code after the dot in a file name (.jpg, .mp4) that says what kind of file it is.
    Hardware
    The physical parts of a computer system you can touch.
    Software
    Programs that run on hardware — apps, games, editors.
    Compatibility
    Whether a file, program or device works together with another.
    Transfer
    Copying a file from one device to another (USB, cloud, attachment, wireless).
    Cloud storage
    Files kept on internet servers (Google Drive, iCloud) so you can open them anywhere.
    Publish
    To put something online where others can see it — happens instantly.
    Digital footprint
    The trail of everything you do online.
    Home row
    The keys A S D F J K L ; where fingers rest when touch-typing.
    WPM
    Words per minute — a measure of typing speed (5 letters = 1 word).

    Did you know?

    • The first spreadsheet program, VisiCalc, came out in 1979 for the Apple II — and it is the reason many businesses bought their first computer.Source: Computer History Museum ↗
    • The bar chart and the line chart were invented by William Playfair in 1786 — before that, numbers were only shown in tables.Source: Britannica ↗
    • Florence Nightingale, the famous nurse, drew “rose” charts in 1858 to show that more soldiers died of disease than of wounds — and her charts changed hospital rules.Source: Science Museum ↗
    • Vietnam’s 2019 census counted 96.2 million people. Enumerators used tablets and phones, so results were ready in weeks instead of years.Source: General Statistics Office ↗
    • Google Forms launched in 2008 as a feature of Google Sheets — the form was invented to feed the spreadsheet, which is still how it works today.Source: Google Workspace Blog ↗

    Points = wins×3 + draws×1: a formula in every row, sorted biggest first.

    Air quality dashboards

    Sensors around Hanoi feed a table every hour; a chart shows when the air is worst — you will program this in Unit 5.

    Glossary

    Data
    Recorded facts: numbers, words, measurements, yes/no answers.
    Information
    Data organised and explained so it answers a question.
    Survey

    Did you know?

    • The word “robot” was invented in 1920 by Czech writer Karel Čapek for his play R.U.R. — from “robota”, meaning hard work.Source: Science Museum ↗
    • The first industrial robot, Unimate, went to work at a General Motors car factory in 1961, lifting hot metal parts that were dangerous for people.Source: Robotics Online (A3) ↗
    • The Roomba vacuum robot came out in 2002; more than 50 million have been sold — the most common robot in people’s homes.Source: iRobot ↗
    • The da Vinci surgical robot (2000) has assisted in more than 10 million operations — a surgeon controls its four arms from a console.Source: Intuitive ↗
    • Tinkercad has more than 100 million registered users, and its models can be printed on a 3D printer straight from the website.Source: Autodesk Tinkercad ↗

    Robots and designers in real life

    Robot vacuum at home

    Bump + cliff sensors, two wheel motors, a brush and a battery — the DustBuddy of the Lab is real.

    Hospital scanners

    A computer turns thousands of X-ray slices into a 3D picture of the body — help for society.

    Automatic doors

    A distance sensor senses you, a controller decides, a motor opens — sense, think, act.

    Photos on the class website

    Cropped to the subject, brightened, shrunk to load fast on a phone.

    3D-printed spare parts

    A broken knob is measured, modelled in Tinkercad and printed in an hour.

    Screen-time limits

    Phones now show a weekly screen-time chart — designers adding a safety rule to their own product.

    Glossary

    Robot
    A machine that senses, thinks (runs a program) and acts by itself.
    Sensor
    A part that measures the world: camera, distance, bump, temperature, light.
    Controller
    The robot’s small computer that runs the program and decides.
    Actuator
    A part that acts: motor, wheel, gripper, speaker.
    Society / individual
    Help for many people at once / help for one person.
    Risk
    A way technology can hurt: screen time, strangers, fake news, unfair decisions.
    Design process
    Problem → user → design → build → test and improve.
    Pixel
    One tiny coloured square of a digital image.
    Crop / resize / rotate
    Cut the edges / change the size / turn the picture.
    Brightness / contrast
    Lighter–darker overall / more difference between dark and light.
    Tinkercad
    Free website for 3D models from shapes; Hole + Group cuts shapes out.
    Prototype
    A first model made to test an idea before building the real thing.

    Did you know?

    • Ada Lovelace wrote the first published computer program in 1843 — for a machine that was never finished. She used variables and a loop, on paper.Source: Computer History Museum ↗
    • The word “algorithm” comes from al-Khwarizmi, who worked in Baghdad’s House of Wisdom around 820 and helped spread the digits 0–9.Source: Britannica ↗
    • The equals sign = was invented in 1557 by Robert Recorde, who chose two parallel lines “because no two things can be more equal”.Source: St Andrews MacTutor ↗
    • The US Air Quality Index scale (0–500, six colours) is used by apps worldwide, including the ones that show Hanoi’s air every hour.Source: AirNow.gov ↗
    • Scratch’s “mod” block and “round” block are the two most used operator blocks in contest solutions — even/odd tests and whole-number answers appear in almost every paper.Source: Scratch Wiki — Operators ↗

    Numbers in programs, in real life

    The air-quality app

    A sensor number → a colour and advice — exactly your unit project, running on a phone.

    Game score

    score is a variable; each coin is “change score by 1”; a new game is “set score to 0”.

    The shop till

    total = price × quantity, change = money − total: the notebook example in real life.

    Countdown timer

    set t to 60 · repeat until t = 0 { wait 1 · change t by −1 } — loops and a counter.

    Fever thermometer

    Ranges again: below 37.5 normal, 37.5–38.5 mild fever, above 38.5 see a doctor.

    Odd/even house numbers

    Postal workers use “number mod 2” without knowing it: odd side, even side.

    Glossary

    Variable
    A named box holding one value that can change.
    set / change by
    set replaces the value; change by adds to it.
    Operator
    A block that calculates: + − × ÷ mod round join.
    mod
    The remainder after division; x mod 2 = 0 means even.
    round / floor
    round → nearest whole number; floor → drop the decimals.
    join
    Glues two pieces of text or numbers into one.
    ask / answer
    ask shows a question; answer holds what was typed — until the next ask.
    Range
    Values between two limits; test with and, or chain if/else.
    AQI
    0–500 in six levels: Good, Moderate, Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups, Unhealthy, Very Unhealthy, Hazardous.
    Counter
    A variable that goes up by 1 each time round a loop.
    repeat until
    Loops until the condition becomes true.
    Edge value
    A value on the boundary of a range — the first thing to test.

    Try it yourself: open an air-quality app or iqair.com/vietnam/hanoi with a parent and read today’s AQI number. Which level is it? What would your program say? Check the number at three different times of day — when is Hanoi’s air worst?

    Did you know?

    • The first internet message was sent on 29 October 1969 between UCLA and Stanford. The student typed “LOGIN” — the system crashed after “LO”.Source: UCLA ↗
    • Undersea cables carry about 99% of international internet traffic. There are roughly 600 active or planned cable systems on the ocean floor.Source: TeleGeography ↗
    • In 2024 about 5.5 billion people — 68% of the world — were online, and 18.8 billion “things” (sensors, cameras, cars) were connected to the Internet of Things.Source: ITU / IoT Analytics ↗
    • Vietnam had about 78.4 million internet users in early 2024 — 79% of the population — and nearly every one of them reaches the internet through a router.Source: DataReportal ↗
    • Satellite tags on dolphins send a position each time the animal surfaces; NOAA scientists have tracked bottlenose dolphins for months this way to protect their habitat.Source: NOAA Fisheries ↗

    Networks in real life

    The box under the TV

    The ISP’s box is router + switch + access point in one — count its cable ports and its antennas.

    School Wi-Fi

    Dozens of access points on the ceiling, one LAN, one router to the ISP — a bigger version of home.

    Google Drive

    Your class photos live on a server; every device asks that server for a copy.

    A video call

    Thousands of packets a second in both directions — the reason calls stutter on weak Wi-Fi.

    GPS in a car

    The car RECEIVES from satellites to find itself; a dolphin tag also SENDS to satellites.

    Weather buoys at sea

    Sensors on buoys send temperature and waves by satellite — the same design as the Dolphin Tracking Center.

    Glossary

    Network
    Devices connected to share data, printers or internet.
    LAN / WAN
    One building / networks joined over distance.
    Internet / ISP
    The network of networks / the company that connects you to it.
    Router
    Connects networks and chooses the route for each packet.
    Switch
    Joins wired devices inside one LAN.
    Access point
    Joins wireless devices to the LAN.
    Server / client
    Stores and serves data / uses the network.
    Wired / wireless
    Cable or fibre / radio waves (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, mobile, satellite).
    Packet
    A small numbered piece of data with a destination address.
    IP address
    A device’s number on the network, e.g. 192.168.1.12.
    Single point of failure
    One link whose failure breaks everything — add a second.
    Internet of Things
    Sensors and machines that send data over networks.

    Try it yourself: with a parent, find the internet box at home. Count the cable ports and the lights. Which devices use a cable? Then go to Wi-Fi settings on a phone and find the network name. Walk to the furthest room — how many signal bars are left?

    Backup to a file & restore

    Cách hoạt động · How it works

    Desktop Chrome/Edge: on the first Save, pick the folder containing this HTML file — every Save then writes the .json (named after this file + date-time) straight there, and each time the page opens it auto-loads the newest one (if the browser re-asks permission, tap the yellow bar). Phones/other browsers: the file downloads to Downloads; load it back with the yellow button.

    🌐 Get backup online (Google Drive or public GitHub)

    Thiết lập một lần (chỉ phụ huynh) · One-time setup (parent only)

    A public GitHub repo needs NOTHING extra — just paste the repo link (github.com/user/repo or …/tree/branch/folder). Google Drive only: browsers block webpages from reading Drive directly (CORS), so an API key is needed — create it free ONCE at console.cloud.google.com (project → enable the Google Drive API → Credentials → API key, with NO referrer restriction). It can only read public files. Share the Drive folder as "Anyone with the link — Viewer". Paste the key below — it is remembered and included in backups, so the child and other devices never need to touch this section.
